articles.title: How did past Super El Niños affect the Philippines?
articles.summary: Here’s a look back on the effects that the past three ‘very strong’ El Niño events had on the country’s agriculture, economy, and health

blocks.text: A “very strong” El Niño — informally called Super El Niño — is expected to start causing droughts in the Philippines by the end of November and continue until March 2027.

This phenomenon can have two critical impacts, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) has warned. On one hand, dry spells and drought will threaten agriculture, water supply, and the broader economy. On the other, short-term but heavy rainfall may still affect the western parts of the country.

blocks.caption: FAST FACTS: What is a Super El Niño, and what should we expect from it?

blocks.text: The Philippines is no stranger to this devastating climate event. The United Nations (UN) said that going by its experiences with past El Niño events, the country has a “strong and well-established sensitivity” to this phenomenon.

According to the World Meteorological Organization, at least three “very strong” El Niños in the past had been as strong, based on the US-based National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI): 1982 to 1983, 1997 to 1998, and 2015 to 2016.

All these events have had a RONI of 2.0°C and above for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods, making them “very strong” El Niños. They occur roughly every 10-15 years, according to the World Resources Institute.
And while the 2026-2027 El Niño is projected to outpace the records set by these previous climate events, looking back on past Super El Niños can give a glimpse of what’s to come.
This El Niño was the largest event in a hundred years, according to the UN Department of Humanitarian Affairs. Based on the latest data as of November 2026, it had a peak RONI of +2.4°C.

It was said to have caused droughts on almost every continent, as well as floods and cyclones, especially in the Pacific. The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution attributed an estimated 1,300 to 2,000 deaths and more than US$13 billion in damage to property and livelihoods to this devastating El Niño event.

The intense climate event came as a surprise, as scientists at the time were unable to predict its onslaught, according to Carbon Brief. A Washington Post report said only a few meteorologists and oceanographers had even heard of El Niño back then.

In the Philippines, the drought conditions brought on by this bout of El Niño affected 19% of the entire country over a period of more than nine months, according to the UN University’s (UNU) 2000 report.

The UNU said that the Visayas and Mindanao were worst hit, where crop failures of rice and corn were documented. On the flip side, flooding caused by excessive monsoon rains and tropical cyclones during this time also damaged rice and corn crops in Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, the Bicol provinces, Western Samar, and Northern Leyte.
The same report found that coconut and sugarcane production was also severely affected. Water reservoirs were almost depleted, affecting hydropower supply and irrigation water.

Overall, this drought caused an estimated $450 million in losses, according to a 2009 study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS). This study and a 2019 World Bank Group report quantified these total losses as follows:

items: a loss of 640,000 metric tons of rice and corn
insurance claims mounting to P38 million
hydropower generation loss of P316 million
450,000 hectares of affected farmland

blocks.text: A large fire also erupted in a rainforest in Mindanao, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reported, adding that prolonged droughts can make certain forest vegetation types prone to disturbance by wildfires. A 2014 SunStar report looking back on these events also reported how farmers witnessed food shortages and wildfires.

Just a little more than a decade later, another very strong El Niño hit, reaching a peak RONI of +2.3°C. Globally, this phenomenon killed some 21,000 people and caused damage to infrastructure worth $36 billion, according to the World Food Program and FAO.

In the Philippines, this El Niño made a devastating impact, causing drought in 68% of the country, compared to only 28% in 1972 and 16% in 1982. The World Bank’s 2019 report said that total agricultural losses then totaled around $87 million.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from the World Bank Group’s 2019 report, “Striking a Balance: Managing El Niño and La Niña in Philippines’ Agriculture.”

blocks.text: The UNU’s 2000 report also listed the following effects:
Water supply

items: dwindling water supply for urban and rural households in many parts of the country

the Angat Dam servicing Metro Manila reached critically low levels, resulting in drastic measures being taken: water supply was reduced by approximately 10%, and service was shortened by four hours daily

blocks.text: Forest fires

items: forest fires burned 9,400 hectares of second growth and logged over forest — including in Palawan, where some endangered species live — equivalent to an estimated P150 million in damages.

blocks.text: Health

items: outbreaks of malaria, dengue or H-fever, diarrhea, and cholera reported by early 1998
acute malnutrition, especially among indigenous peoples
72 reported deaths, with 42 due to food poisoning from eating root crops not well-prepared for human consumption

blocks.text: The World Bank’s 2019 report also pointed out that another factor that made this El Niño event unique was its overlap with the Asian financial crisis.
“These losses compounded the human and economic consequences from the financial crisis,” the group wrote in their report.
The World Bank and UNU listed the following economic effects:

items: GDP growth slowing to only 1.2% in the second quarter of 1998, which was the economy’s worst performance since 1992
P7.24 billion in fisheries losses as of November 1998
total power generation from hydropower plants dropped from 19% in 1992 to 1% in 1998, owing to hydroelectric plants suffering considerable deficits due to a decrease in water supply
an increase in poverty from 25% in 1997 to 28% in 1998, which the World Bank said was more attributable to El Niño agricultural shocks than the Asian financial crisis

blocks.text: Less than a decade later, another very strong El Niño formed, reaching a peak RONI of +2.3°C. Around the world, the event severely affected more than 60 million people, according to the UN. It was one of the factors that made 2015 the hottest year on record, during which more than 7,000 people died from heat waves, based on a 2016 UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction report.

The 18-month El Niño started in February 2015 and ended in July 2016, and caused damage across 85% of the Philippines, according to the April 2019 National Drought Plan for the Philippines. Luzon and Mindanao were said to have borne the brunt of the damages.
This plan listed the following effects brought on by the El Niño event:

items: P10 billion in crop damages
1.48 million metric tons of crops lost, including rice, corn, cassava, banana, and rubber
over 400,000 farming households and 556,000 hectares affected
23% decline in fish catch due to warmer waters, suggesting at least 100,000 fisherfolk would need to look for alternative sources of income
P600 million in defensive expenditures
low dam water levels, where 9 out of 25 dams dried up, 6 were at critical levels, and 10 were below normal water levels
prevalence of disease due to malnutrition and reduced access to potable water
approximately 25% of households in Mindanao reported poor food consumption, according to a March 2016 survey

blocks.text: A 2026 UN report said that drought impacts were compounded by pest outbreaks, including rat infestations.

Another UN report from 2017 estimated that total losses may have been as high as $11 billion. This report added that the severe economic impact and perceived lack of government action led to protests.

The most infamous of these protests were the Kidapawan protests that happened on April 1, 2016. The unrest turned violent, which left two protesters dead, two police officers seriously wounded, and 179 farmers and police officers injured, according to the Commission on Human Rights.

blocks.caption: Kidapawan and the rice riots

blocks.text: The present Super El Niño is set to break records set by its predecessors, with the NOAA Climate Prediction Center November 2026 advisory saying there is an estimated 60% chance for the RONI to be 2.5°C or more for the October-December and November-January periods.
Locally, this El Niño is expected to virtually put the entire country at risk of drought by March 2027.
Has the Philippines and its government learned its lessons from Super El Niños past? – Rappler.com

articles.title: Francis called Tagle ‘a saint’ and ‘kindness incarnate,’ book on late pope’s diary says
articles.summary: Pope Francis once described Luis Antonio Cardinal Tagle as “a saint who possesses the best of Asian qualities—kindness incarnate,” according to a new book by one of the late…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 1:32pm

MANILA, Philippines — Pope Francis once described Luis Antonio Cardinal Tagle as “a saint who possesses the best of Asian qualities—kindness incarnate,” according to a new book by one of the late pontiff’s closest confidantes that draws on a diary Francis kept for more than three decades.
Cardinal Víctor Manuel “Tucho” Fernández, who compiled and annotated "The Private Diary of Pope Francis," recalls the remark from his own conversations with the late pontiff.
He cites it as an example of how the pope spoke well of his collaborators in the Roman Curia “even when someone tried to provoke him into expressing criticism.”
The 160-page book was released on Tuesday, November 24, in five languages and 94 countries by the Vatican Publishing House. Pope Francis died at age 88 on April 21, 2025.
In the same passage, Fernández, who heads the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, recalls Francis’s praise for four other senior churchmen.

The late pope said Cardinal Robert Prevost — now Pope Leo XIV, whom he brought to Rome in 2023 to lead the office that vets bishop appointments — had always been “a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man.”
Francis also called Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, “an excellent diplomat, the cardinal who best understood international politics.”

Francis also spoke well of two cardinals widely seen as critics of his papacy. He described Guinea’s Cardinal Robert Sarah as a believer “with a refined spiritual sensitivity” and said Germany’s Cardinal Gerhard Müller “seems aggressive, but he’s a good man, but good, good.”
Francis had declined to renew Müller’s term as the Vatican’s doctrine chief in 2017 and accepted Sarah’s resignation as head of its worship office in 2021.
Dean of the cardinals
Tagle was himself viewed as part of the inner circle of the late Pope Francis and had worked closely with him for most of his 12-year papacy.
As archbishop of Manila, Tagle hosted the Francis' January 2015 visit, when 6 million to 7 million people attended the closing Mass at Rizal Park, a record for a papal event.
Francis brought Tagle to Rome in 2019 to lead the Vatican’s missionary office, and in 2022 named him pro-prefect of its section for first evangelization, the post he still holds under Pope Leo.
Tagle is also dean of the College of Cardinals, a position he was elected to in October, making him the first Asian prelate to hold the post.
Often dubbed in Catholic media as the “Asian Francis,” Tagle was among the most discussed contenders to succeed Francis before the May 2025 conclave, which elected Prevost.
Pope Francis kept long-term diary
Francis wrote intermittently in a black-covered planner for the year 1992 that he never used for appointments, according to Fernández.
The entries run from Dec. 20, 1992 — the year he was named auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires — to Aug. 18, 2024, eight months before his death.
In all, Francis filled 86 pages before his 2013 election and 55 as pope.
The most confidential matters are written in code, “using symbols that we cannot and should not decipher,” Fernández writes.
He says he also left out details that directly affect third parties and, in some cases, names.
Fernández says Francis showed him the notebook at the Casa Santa Marta, the Vatican guesthouse where the pope lived, telling him: “From this, you will all see.”
A few weeks after Leo’s election, Fernández told the new pope he feared the writings “might end up abandoned in a warehouse somewhere.” Leo sent him the cardboard box of papers days later.
Fernández writes that he ultimately spent a year preparing the book.
Crisis and ‘the entrance to hell’
International media outlets have widely focused on Francis’s account of his own spiritual struggles as detailed in his diary.

According to the book, the Argentine pope went through a crisis from January 2021 to December 2022, as his health worsened, connected to what he saw as a temptation to exercise power over others. In a December 2022 entry, he described it as “all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation.”

He also wrote that he believed he had seen the devil three times, once during a meeting after returning to Rome. In an entry dated June 7, 2018, as the scale of the clergy sexual abuse scandal in Chile became clear to him, he wrote: “Last night I saw the entrance to hell.” He added that he “grabbed the Rosary as a weapon.”

Fernández cautions against reading this as proof that Francis was manipulative. “It is not easy to find an important event that took place between 2021 and 2022 in which he outwardly manifested what he so deeply regretted,” he writes, calling the experience “more internal than external.”
‘Like a delicate crystal’

The remarks about Tagle, Prevost, Parolin and other cardinals appear in a chapter on what Fernández calls Francis’s “unshakable” conviction about human dignity, or the belief that every person “must be treated like a delicate crystal.”
Fernández writes that during meetings or meals, Francis was “evidently upset if someone present treated an employee impolitely or spoke to another person sarcastically.”

Elsewhere, Fernández recounts that Francis grew fond of an immigrant woman who worked at Santa Marta. One morning he was told she had died suddenly. Minutes later, a visiting president arrived, and some media outlets read the pope’s downcast face as a sign of disrespect.
Fernández also writes that he once told Francis he was “quite hard of hearing” and asked how he answered questions he had not fully heard.
“My intuition saves me,” the pope replied, according to Fernández.
That intuition, Fernández says, explains why Francis “would sometimes say one thing and in other contexts seem to say something different” — a complaint long raised by his critics.
Popular piety
The book also takes up a subject close to Filipino Catholics: Francis’s regard for popular piety, the devotions and traditions ordinary believers practice outside formal liturgy.

Fernández writes that during his years as a bishop in Latin America, Francis drew on the document produced by the region’s bishops at Puebla, Mexico, in 1979, which treated popular religion as an expression of a people’s culture.
In his personal copy, Francis underlined passages on “the new valuation of popular religiosity” but not a phrase referring to its “distortions and ambiguities.”
“He was tired of the criticism directed at popular piety coming from certain sectors, both traditionalists and progressives,” Fernández writes.
In the Philippines, such devotions draw millions every year, among them the Traslacion of the Black Nazarene in Manila and the Sinulog festival in Cebu honoring the Santo Niño.

Francis tied the Santo Niño to Filipino family life in a video message for the 500th anniversary of Christianity in the country, released by the Vatican on April 4, 2021. Francis said the image of the Holy Child, “a symbol of the arrival of Christianity in your archipelago,” recalls the hidden life of the Holy Family in Nazareth. — With reports by Ian Laqui

articles.title: BCDA commits to no Pax Silica evictions until funds, rights secured
articles.summary: The Bases Conversion and Development Authority has told senators it would not displace residents, clear farmland, or relocate communities for the US-backed Pax Silica hub in Tarlac until funds are…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 1:13pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Bases Conversion and Development Authority has told senators it would not displace residents, clear farmland, or relocate communities for the US-backed Pax Silica hub in Tarlac until funds are secured and residents' rights are respected.

This commitment — made amid mounting criticism of the lack of transparency on the aims and design of the hub, as well as harassment of its critics — was delivered through Sen. Bam Aquino, sponsor of the BCDA's proposed 2027 budget, during plenary debate of the proposed spending plan late Tuesday, November 24.
The BCDA was asked by Sen. Imee Marcos on which agency would fund the relocation of the Aeta and farming families living on the 1,620-hectare planned manufacturing hub in Capas town.
Aquino, relaying the BCDA's answer, said the agency had no estimate yet of what compensation would cost but that future investors in the zone would shoulder the cost.
During plenary debates on the budget, agencies can only answer questions through their designated sponsor on the floor.

"So the BCDA categorically commits that no resident will be displaced, no agricultural land will be cleared, and no community be relocated [until] funds are secured and their rights are acknowledged and respected," Marcos said.
"Yes, there's a commitment," Aquino said.
The Philippines joined Pax Silica, an initiative by the US government to secure supply chains for semiconductors, artificial intelligence and critical minerals and reduce reliance on China, in April.
The government has since set aside a 1,620-hectare "Economic Security Zone" inside New Clark City, on state land administered by the BCDA, which now calls it the Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park.
The plan has met opposition from the Aeta Hungey of Sitio Sapang Kawayan, who have sought recognition of their ancestral domain since 1994, and from farmers in neighboring Barangay O'Donnell.

Rights watchdog Human Rights Watch estimates the hub would displace hundreds of people and that available information indicated the BCDA had not obtained the community's free, prior and informed consent.
Who pays

The BCDA's proposed 2027 budget does not set aside specific funds for the Pax Silica site. However, upon questioning by Sen. Imee Marcos, it confirmed that it may use its corporate funds as "financial assistance" for those that may be displaced.
Aquino, relaying BCDA's answer, said there is "P322 million allocated for financial assistance... This is not particularly in the areas affected by Pax Silica. This is in all BCDA areas."
"But if ever there would be assistance to the families there, it would be coming from this budget... It's in their corporate funds," Aquino said.

Asked whether the BCDA had estimated what it would cost to compensate families for the loss of homes, farmland, crops and livelihoods, and whether P322 million would be enough, Aquino said there was no estimate yet.

However, it would ultimately be the private firms setting up shop, or the "locators," who have to shoulder the cost of transferring residents to a new location and compensating them for any loss of livelihood and income.
It is the locators who would fund the financial support programs, while the BCDA would handle consultations and "social preparation," Aquino said.

This did not sit well with Marcos, who questioned whether this amounted to leaving residents' welfare to private companies. "Eh kung 'yung commercial entity lang ang papasok, sinong lalaban para sa kanila?" she asked. (If only a commercial entity comes in, who will fight for them?)
Aquino said the BCDA would handle residents' concerns while investors paid for the physical development of the site.
Changing numbers of affected. Senators have also flagged the changing numbers of how many actual residents would be affected by the industrial zone.
Aquino said the BCDA's official figure now stood at 198 families, down from close to 400 cited at a Senate hearing in August, while the latest reports place it nearer 1,000.
He said an independent body such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development or the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) should help identify who would be affected.
Quitclaims and relocation
Marcos also told BCDA that senators have received reports from residents who notices to vacate and had been asked to sign quitclaims and waivers for the development of the hub.
Aquino said the BCDA denied asking individuals to sign a quitclaim and was still in talks with affected residents. Marcos said the evidence should be taken up at another hearing.
Human Rights Watch reported this month that farmers in Sitio Binyayan had been offered about P300,000 per hectare and given 10 to 30 days to respond.

Marcos also cited estimates that the hub would need 3 gigawatts of electricity, about 16 percent of Luzon grid capacity, a figure the BCDA itself has used. Aquino said the BCDA acknowledged the figure but planned to generate power on site rather than draw from the grid.
"No power plants are made in two years. Everything takes about five years," Aquino said, adding that this meant investors would likely not locate in the zone for about five years.
Shifting plans

Aquino, though sponsoring the budget, himself criticized the agency's changing descriptions of the project. "Nagsimula 'yan with data center, marami hong umalma... And then suddenly in the hearing wala nang data center. Naging manufacturing pero hindi rin malinaw kung anong klase," he said. (It started as a data center and many objected to that... Then suddenly at the hearing there was no data center. It became manufacturing, but it was not clear what kind.)
"It is important that things are clear to the public and not just to those directly involved, but to all of us. What exactly are we getting ourselves into?" Aquino said in mixed English and Filipino.
"It should be clear to us what the agreements and negotiations entail, and we need to understand exactly what we are entering into here with the United States," he added.
Marcos called for a second Senate hearing on the project and said a follow-up to the first inquiry was long overdue.
The Senate voted in September to constitute itself as a committee of the whole, presided over by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, to take up the resolutions filed on Pax Silica.

articles.title: [In This Economy] Dapat ka bang singilin dahil sa utang ng Pilipinas?
articles.summary: Wala tayong kanya-kanyang bill na katumbas ng 'utang kada Pilipino'

blocks.text: Umani ng kontrobersya ang pahayag ni Senador Alan Peter Cayetano noong September 23 sa umpisa ng plenary sessions sa pagtalakay sa 2027 budget.
Pinalutang kasi niya ang ideyang kusang mag-ambag ang mga Pilipino ng mahigit P170,000 bawat isa.

Ito ay bunsod ng mga ulat na sa P19.66 trilyon ang utang ng pambansang gobyerno sa pagtatapos ng Setyembre 2026, ayon sa Bureau of the Treasury. Katumbas ’yan ng 66.9% ng GDP, mula sa 66% noong katapusan ng Hunyo.
Sa madaling salita, lumaki na talaga ang utang kumpara sa laki ng ekonomiya.
Ang pahayag ni Cayetano ay pinatulan naman ng media. Sa iba’t ibang ulat, pinukaw ang atensyon ng mga tao sa tanong na, “Magkano ang utang ng bawat Pilipino?”
Ang sagot umano ay P174,405.06. Nakuha ’yan sa paghahati ng utang ng gobyerno sa populasyong naitala sa 2024 census.
Ngunit may pakiusap ako sa media at sa mga politiko. Tuwing lumalabas ang bagong datos sa utang ng gobyerno, tigilan na po sana natin ang pagsasabing “ganito na kalaki ang utang ng bawat Pilipino.”

Alam ko naman kung bakit patok ang linyang ’yan. Mahirap arukin kung gaano kalaki ang isang trilyong piso. Kapag hinati mo ang utang sa dami ng Pilipino, mas relatable ang halaga at mas madaling isama sa headline.
Ngunit ang implikasyon ng ganitong numero ay pati ang mga sanggol na kapapanganak lang ay may utang na dapat bayaran. At pinapahiwatig din na pwedeng singilin ang bawat Pilipino. Maling-mali ito!
Tandaan na gobyerno ang umutang. Gobyerno rin ang may obligasyong magbayad.

Siyempre, apektado tayong mga ordinaryong mamamayan dahil sa buwis din natin nanggagaling ang malaking bahagi ng perang ginagamit ng gobyerno para magbayad. Bukod diyan, kapag lumalaki ang kinakain ng interes sa budget, mas kaunti ang perang puwedeng ilaan sa mga silid-aralan, ospital, at iba pang serbisyo.
Pero wala tayong kanya-kanyang bill na katumbas ng “utang kada Pilipino.”

Misleading ang debt per person na numero. Kasi kung pareho lang ang utang ng gobyerno at dumami ang populasyon, bababa agad ang utang kada tao. Pero may nabayaran ba ang gobyerno? Wala. Nadagdagan ba agad ang koleksiyon ng buwis? Wala rin. Bumaba ang numero dahil dumami ang pinaghati-hatian.

Kaya ang mas magandang tanong na dapat nating sagutin ay: Sustainable ba ang utang? At kaya bang tugunan ng gobyerno ang mga obligasyon nito sa paglipas ng panahon nang hindi napipilitang magtaas nang husto ng buwis o magbawas nang malaki sa mahahalagang serbisyo?

blocks.caption: Source: Bureau of Treasury

blocks.text: Dito pumapasok ang konsepto ng “debt-to-GDP ratio.”
Kinukumpara nito ang kabuuang utang sa gross domestic product o GDP, ang halaga ng mga produkto at serbisyong nalilikha ng ekonomiya sa loob ng isang taon.
Halimbawa, kung P15 trilyon ang utang at P25 trilyon ang GDP, 60% ang ratio.

Kung tumaas ang utang sa P16 trilyon pero lumaki ang GDP sa P28 trilyon, bababa ang ratio sa mga 57%. Lumaki ang utang sa piso, pero mas mabilis lumaki ang ekonomiyang pinanggagalingan ng kita at buwis.

Walang namang awtomatikong “safe” na numero. Magkaiba ang sitwasyon ng dalawang gobyernong pareho ang debt-to-GDP ratio kung mas mataas ang interes na binabayaran ng isa, o kung mas maliit ang nakokolekta nitong buwis.
Kaya mahalaga ring tingnan kung pataas o pababa ang debt-to-GDP ratio at kung gaano kalaki sa kita ng gobyerno ang napupunta sa interes.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] The Philippines has entered stagflation territory

blocks.text: May isa pang paghahambing na madalas gamitin ng mga ekonomista, at ito ang r vs. g.
Ang r ay ang average na interes sa utang ng gobyerno, at ang g ay ang bilis ng paglago ng ekonomiya.
Kapag mas mabilis lumaki ang ekonomiya kaysa sa interes sa utang, mas madaling pigilan ang pagtaas ng debt-to-GDP ratio. Kapag mas mataas naman ang interes kaysa sa paglago, mas mahirap.
At kahit paborable ang agwat, puwede pa ring tumaas ang debt ratio kung taon-taon ay mas malaki ang gastos ng gobyerno kaysa sa kita nito, kahit ibukod pa ang bayad sa interes.
Panghuli, at marahil pinaka-importante, dapat ding tanungin: Saan napunta ang inutang?

‘Di naman kasi masama ang umutang. Kung ginamit sa tulay na nagpapababa ng gastos sa pagbiyahe at pagdadala ng produkto, may pakinabang na puwedeng tumagal nang maraming taon. Ngunit kung napunta sa proyektong binayaran pero wala palang naitayo (aka “ghost projects”), taon din nating babayaran ang interes.

Kaya sa susunod na maglabas ng datos sa utang, ito ang itanong natin sa mga opisyal: Gaano kalaking bahagi ng kita ng gobyerno ang kinakain ng interes? Sa bilis ng paglago ngayon, saan papunta ang debt-to-GDP ratio? At ano ang naipagawa o naibigay sa publiko gamit ang perang inutang?
Mas may silbi sa mga Pilipino ang mga sagot diyan, kaysa sa isa na namang click-baity headline na may utang daw ang bawat isa sa atin. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

articles.title: Supreme Court should have ruled on legality of Duterte's ICC arrest — Leonen
articles.summary: In his concurring and dissenting opinion on the ruling, while Leonen agreed to dismiss the petition due to its mootness, he pointed out that the High Court missed an opportunity to establish clear…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 1:03pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court should have ruled on the habeas corpus petition filed by former President Rodrigo Duterte challenging his arrest and transfer to the International Criminal Court, Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen said.

In his 58-page concurring and dissenting opinion on the ruling, Leonen agreed to dismiss the petition on the ground of mootness but pointed out that the high court missed an opportunity to establish clear guidelines on how international arrest warrants must be executed under the Constitution.

“Summary or extrajudicial killings sponsored by an administration of government are consequential. They impact not only our country but the international community as well. We should take judicial notice that, when sponsored by an administration of government with widespread consequences, its principal perpetrators can be many, and thus arrest and surrender to the International Criminal Court is capable of repetition. That the person of an accused will be surrendered to an International Criminal Court in The Hague means it can evade our review. It can evade review, especially when done in the manner done to the Petitioner in this case. Thus, I cannot agree that we dismiss the Petition by simply declaring that it is moot. That may be politically expedient. That approach tends to undermine our legitimacy as the Court of last resort if we do not provide the clearest guidelines for the bench and bar and, by implication, our law enforcement agencies on the application of the protection of human rights in our laws and the Rome Statute as read through our Constitution.”

The consolidated petitions for a writ of habeas corpus—filed by Duterte’s children, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, Veronica and Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City 1st District)—challenged the legality of the former president's arrest and subsequent transfer to The Hague.

The majority of the Supreme Court justices dismissed the petitions as moot, given that the former president is already in the physical custody of the ICC, which has the competence to determine its own jurisdiction.
Leonen, however, warned that simply declaring the petitions moot is a "politically expedient" cop-out that undermines the Supreme Court's legitimacy as the court of last resort.

“The constitutional issues raised in the present Petitions are grave and serious and capable of repetition, yet evading review. This case cannot simply be dismissed on the ground of mootness, even if doing so may be the politically expedient resolution,” Leonen said.

“As the Court of last resort, we must not shirk our duty of providing the clearest guidelines for the bench and the bar and, by implication, our law enforcement agencies. That is the resolution that would best safeguard and operationalize the human rights provisions under the Rome Statute, which are read through our Constitution,” he added.

Because the former president’s alleged co-perpetrators remain at large in the Philippines and could face similar sudden arrests and transfers, Leonen insisted that the Supreme Court must issue authoritative guidelines to govern future cases.

“It will shape how our trial courts treat the next person arrested for surrender to an international tribunal, and how lawyers advise the officers who make the arrest. If we do the expedient thing and leave the question unanswered, we teach the bench and the bar that comfort, convenience, and the political agenda of the day may decide what due process requires. That would be a lesson in a lesser version of our profession, and this Court should not be the one to teach it,” Leonen said.

"While upholding the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction to prosecute his offenses, this Court should also have made clear that the manner of his surrender was inconsistent with our own legal order," he added.
Hasty arrest
Duterte was taken into custody at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport on March 11, 2025, based on an ICC arrest warrant and an Interpol diffusion request.
Within hours, he was placed on a plane destined for The Hague, with custody officially transferred to the ICC by the following day.
Leonen pointed out that this rapid-fire transfer completely bypassed local judicial systems, violating Duterte's right to due process under the Constitution.

Under Article 59 of the Rome Statute—which remains binding on the Philippines for acts committed prior to its 2019 withdrawal—any person arrested under an ICC warrant must be brought "promptly" before a competent judicial authority in the custodial state.

Leonen argued that Philippine authorities were duty-bound to present Duterte before a local court to verify his identity, ensure proper process was followed, and confirm his constitutional rights were respected.

“Moreover, because he was arrested and surrendered on the same day (March 11, 2025), former President Duterte was also completely deprived of his lawful opportunity under Article 59(3) of the Rome Statute to apply to any competent domestic authority for interim release pending surrender to the International Criminal Court,” Leonen said.

“The principal constitutional defect lay not in the absence of a fresh determination of probable cause that question belonged to the issuing international court or tribunal but in the total absence of any judicial review: former President Duterte was taken and flown to The Hague within hours, without any judicial imprimatur sought by his captors. That omission was a real violation of his right to be free from seizure except through judicial process,” he added.
Protecting the powerless
Leonen acknowledged that Duterte is widely despised by many for the alleged summary executions committed during his administration's "war on drugs.”
He noted that denying Duterte due process might "win wide acclaim" and satisfy those seeking accountability.
However, Leonen cautioned that the Supreme Court cannot decide cases based on political comfort or visceral temptation.
He stressed that the legal procedures bypassed in Duterte's arrest are the same safeguards that protect ordinary citizens.
"The procedure that protects a former president is the same procedure that protects the farmer taken at night and the young father picked up in an operation in a crowded barangay," Leonen said.
"Whatever we refuse to the powerful, we will soon be unable to guarantee to the powerless,” he added.

articles.title: In charts: how power could shift in Europe’s big year of elections
articles.summary:
More than half of EU voters will go to the polls in the next 12 months, with the far right targeting significant gains. We set out the political landscape and trends

Over the coming 12…
articles.byline: Jon Henley, Jakub Krupa and Seán Clarke

blocks.text: Over the coming 12 months, more than half of the EU’s electorate will go to the polls in elections that could change the direction of the continent, with attention focused on voters in four of the bloc’s five biggest states.

In Spain, France and Poland, elections could bring the far right into government. Italy’s far-right prime minister looks likely to remain in power, but is under pressure from a challenger even more to the right.

While few of Europe’s far-right parties want to leave the EU, they still see the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty and are bent on transforming it into something far looser.

The graphics below map the main political parties in each country along two ideological axes – economic left-right and libertarian-authoritarian – using data from researchers at the Chapel Hill Expert Survey. Polling averages then show how the race is developing.
Spain
Parliamentary election on 29 November
Spain will head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government.

Since the restoration of democracy in Spain in 1977, every prime minister has come from one of three parties: the now-disbanded Union of the Democratic Centre, a very broad centrist alliance from the time of the transition; the centre-right People’s party (PP); and the centre-left Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE).

Often the ruling party has needed the support of smaller parties, sometimes regional groups. But, as elsewhere in Europe, the traditional centre-right and centre-left parties are being challenged by populists further to the left and right.

Since 2023, Pedro Sánchez has been in government with the support of Sumar, which sits ideologically to the left of his PSOE party. But polling suggests that PSOE and Sumar’s latest incarnation, Broad Front, will together fail to muster a majority in parliament.

That leaves the door partly open to the PP, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, but he too will need support, and just as Sánchez looked to his left, it is thought Feijóo will look to his right, bringing the far-right Vox of Santiago Abascal into government. Abascal this week told a rally that “remigration sounds to me like heavenly music”.
France
Presidential election on 18 April and 2 May 2027

The sitting president, Emmanuel Macron, has served the maximum two terms and will be an onlooker in spring’s election. If, as usual, no candidate wins 50% in the first round of voting, the two leading candidates go into a runoff two weeks later. Polling suggests that Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right Rassemblement National (the National Rally) will be one of those two, for the third time.

But unlike on previous occasions, there is no obvious centrist candidate to challenge her in the second round. The president’s heirs apparent – Gabriel Attal of Macron’s Renaissance party and Édouard Philippe of coalition partners Horizons – are splitting the centrist vote. Both were prime ministers under Macron – but then so were five other politicians.

Raphaël Glucksmann, a former Socialist who left to found his own party, is nonetheless the Socialist and centre-left candidate. He is outflanked on the left by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who seems most likely to face Le Pen in the second round. In the contest between the far left and far right, the polls suggest Le Pen will be the victor.
Poland
Parliamentary election 11 November 2027

For 20 years, the prime ministers of Poland have come from one of two parties, the hard-right Law and Justice (PiS) party, or the Civic Platform – now Civic Coalition (KO) – of Donald Tusk, a centrist and relatively libertarian party which is in government. The two parties’ starkly opposing ideas and practices have led to constitutional crisis, not least because the PiS holds the presidency.

Although polling shows support for the PiS faltering, Tusk can take little comfort – much of that support seems to be flowing toward parties even farther to the right; Konfederacja (Confederation), a libertarian nationalist far-right coalition, and their former allies, the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). KKP was last assessed by Chapel Hill researchers in 2024 as part of Konfederacja, but the party is significantly further to the authoritarian right. It is also the only party that advocates Poland’s withdrawal from the EU and faces regular criticism for pro-Russian positions on foreign policy.

Even worse for Tusk, two of his three coalition partners – the centre-right Polska 2050 and the conservative agrarian PSL – are at risk of polling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament. Their success or failure in clearing that threshold could play a major role in deciding the election.
Italy
Parliamentary election due by 22 December 2027

The last of the big four is Italy, where the far right has been in power since 2022. Giorgia Meloni’s Fratelli d’Italia (Brothers of Italy) party has been in a rightwing coalition with Lega (League) and the relatively centrist Forza Italia.
Meloni is odds on to remain prime minister after the election, according to the Polymarket betting site. But she is under pressure, perhaps surprisingly, from the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a retired general, has started a far-right party, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), and is polling at least as well as Meloni’s coalition partners. Vannacci’s party is too new to have been assessed by Chapel Hill researchers, but given that his stated reason for leaving Lega was that it was insufficiently rightwing, it is very probably in the upper right quadrant of the chart.

articles.title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
articles.summary:
With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate

Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far…
articles.byline: A reporter in southern Yemen and William Christou in Beirut

blocks.text: Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

Today, Hussein is once again considering the painful decision of leaving home. In September, the Iran-aligned Houthis swept aside Yemeni government forces, and now have set their sights on Aden. Houthi fighters are amassing to the north and east of the city, and have begun encircling the government-controlled territory.

blocks.caption: People displaced by war on the Red Sea coastline receive aid near Aden, Yemen. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: “I fled my home in Sana’a and came here. I don’t think the Houthis plan to take over Aden right now, but if they get closer, I will have no choice but to flee again to Marib or Hadhramaut,” said Hussein, who was speaking under a pseudonym.

Hussein works as a schoolteacher and was formerly a member of the Islah party, an Islamist political party aligned with Saudi Arabia that is in opposition to the Houthi movement. He fears that if the Houthis take control of Aden he could face persecution for his former affiliation.
“The Houthis don’t believe in freedom, they just want to hear one voice, the one they like,” he said.

Hussein is one of many residents and organisations nervously watching the Houthi advance. The militia is still about 50 miles (80km) north of Aden, but local people fear government forces may not be able to resist another Houthi assault, having seen the dramatic collapse of government forces and allied militias in September.

blocks.caption: Houthi forces take over from Dhubab to Bab el-Mandeb, Taiz governorate, Yemen, after Saudi-backed forces withdraw from the area, 16 November 2026. Photograph: Houthi Military Media/Reuters

blocks.text: Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government of Yemen since 2015. If the Houthis took the city, it would be a huge blow for the government, and a massive failure for the Saudi-led coalition which has for years fought against the Houthis.
The 12-year-long civil war would tilt dramatically in the Houthis’ favour and be a boon for Iran, which has long invested military and political support in the insurgent movement.

The Yemeni government has pulled back many of its fighters to help defend Aden and the surrounding areas, announcing last week that fighters were redeployed from areas along the south-western coast towards the port city.

Saudi Arabia has tried to halt the Houthi advance with a renewed bombing campaign, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to statistics from the independent Yemen Data Project.
Houthi authorities have alleged that Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July.

blocks.caption: A rescuer walks through the debris of a destroyed building belonging to Yemen’s Public Telecommunications Corporation following a Saudi strike in the port city of Hodeida. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Houthis have not announced any intention to take Aden, but have instead been amassing troops north of Kirish, and in al-Bayda, areas which, if taken, would cut off the northern and eastern roads to Aden.
“The buildups in al-Bayda could threaten Aden’s eastern road links through Abyan and Saudi supply lines into the city,” said Mohammed al-Basha, the founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.

“The Houthis appear to be testing how well Aden’s defences will hold. If they collapse, the Houthis could try to seize the city. If government forces hold, the Houthis could try to lay siege to it,” al-Basha added.

blocks.caption: Members of the National Security Forces at a checkpoint as security is tightened in Aden. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Houthi forces have begun striking Aden and its surrounding areas, rupturing the relative safety the city has offered for years. Residents have watched anxiously as explosions grow nearer, and displaced people from surrounding areas have started to arrive in greater numbers.
“Since last week, we’ve started following the news every hour. When I get busy, I tell my daughter to follow it and update me,” said Rami, a resident of Aden who spoke under a pseudonym.

The 53-year-old bitterly recalled his experience during the four-month battle for Aden in 2015, when he was stuck in the crossfire between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces. He, like other people in Aden, is trying to make his own calculation of when, or if, the Houthis will arrive.
International organisations are also making contingency plans in case of a Houthi takeover of the city.

blocks.caption: A displaced woman carries an aid box at the al-Fardous displacement camp in Ras Imran, on the outskirts of Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: “We were informed by management that they are issuing termination notices to all staff this week. If the Houthis don’t reach Aden, they will continue operations and renew our contracts; otherwise this is the end of the road,” an aid worker with an international NGO said.
Already, several NGOs were forced to shut down in the city of Taiz after sweeping Houthi gains.

Not all NGOs would leave in the case of a Houthi takeover, but some are unable to work in Houthi-controlled areas either due to fears for the safety of aid workers, or because the US Treasury designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025.
Yemen has for years faced a severe humanitarian crisis, with about 18.7 million people facing acute food insecurity.

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemenis from the west coast wait to receive medical care at Prince Mohammed bin Salman hospital in Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Fighting has only exacerbated conditions, severing transport routes, pushing up the prices of goods and worsening the country’s displacement crisis – including more than 350,000 people displaced since August.

“I earn daily wages, and when there is no work, my six family members don’t get enough food,” said Ahmed, a restaurant worker in his 50s. “I don’t care about politics or wars, and I’m not involved in any of it. I’m just like millions of Yemenis struggling to provide basic necessities for their families.”
For many of Aden’s residents, the prospect of a Houthi takeover has shattered the sense of safety that they sought by coming to the government stronghold in the first place.

“I’m not stocking up on food because I won’t stay in Aden and wait for the battles to reach the city. It isn’t only me; my family is also ready to flee at any time … staying at home won’t be safe and we might get trapped,” Rami said.

articles.title: India news: US prepares new tariffs after trade probe
articles.summary: The United States is reportedly readying fresh tariffs on India and 15 other economies under a trade probe. Also, a woman was allegedly gangraped by her colleagues in the national capital. Follow…

image.caption: India and the US are yet to finalize a trade dealImage: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: Live

The United States is reportedly readying fresh tariffs on India and 15 other economies under a trade probe. Also, a woman was allegedly gangraped by her colleagues in the national capital. Follow live.
Prefer DW on Google

blocks.caption: India and the US are yet to finalize a trade dealImage: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: USTR set to unveil results of a probe on excess industrial capacity in India and 15 other economies
Probe could lead to fresh tariffs on India and others
Woman allegedly gangraped in Delhi by her colleagues

blocks.text: Here are the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, November 25:
November 25, 2026
US set to unveil new tariffs after probe on excess factory capacity

India could be one of the 16 countries facing fresh and imminent US tariffs with the Trump administration set to release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacities, Reuters reported citing three people with knowledge of the matter.
The results of the investigation are likely to be released over the course of the day, followed by new import duties on a wide range of goods if the probe find India guilty of excess capacity.
It remains unclear what tariff rates would be proposed but one of the sources told the news agency that they would be specifically tailored to each country.
That said, the US is likely to honor capped tariff rates agreed on in finalized US trade deals with partner countries.
A report by the Wall Street Journal said that India could face higher US tariffs than economies like Japan or the European Union.
Where are US tariffs on India?

The US introduced 25% reciprocal tariffs in 2025 on India, under US President Donald Trump's second term. The rate was later lowered to 18% with Washington and New Delhi agreeing to an interim trade framework while a more comprehensive trade agreement would be worked on. Leaders from both nations have since said the first tranche of a trade agreement was "close," but a deal remains elusive.

Meanwhile in July 2026, the United States Trade Representative (USTR), which carries out trade-related investigations, imposed an additional 10% tariffs on India and other countries after a probe on traded goods made using forced labor.

articles.title: Libya: 2 dead after Ukrainian attack on Russian warship in Benghazi
articles.summary: The head of the eastern administration in Libya has confirmed that two Libyan soldiers succumbed to their injures. Ukraine's foreign minister defended the attack as an effort to counter Russian…

image.caption: The Ukrainian military released footage of the naval drone attack in BenghaziImage: Security Service of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two Libyan soldiers have died from their injuries sustained during a Ukrainian attack on a Russian warship in docked in the port of Benghazi.
Libya is currently divided between a UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east of the country that controls Benghazi.
The head of the eastern administration, Oussama Hamad, said the two men had died "as a result of their injuries during the treacherous Ukrainian aggression against the port of Benghazi."

blocks.caption: The attack sunk a Russian Navy corvetteImage: Vantor/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Libyan National Army General Command said a response would come "at the appropriate time and place."
Earlier, on Monday, Libya's Foreign ministry denounced the attacks and said it didn't authorize "any foreign military operations within [Libya's] territory or territorial waters.
Ukraine denies dragging Libya into war
The naval drone attack that occurred on Sunday was claimed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday. On Tuesday, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha defended the attack.
"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Sybiha said on Telegram.

"Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended ‌to harm Libya or its people."
He said Russia was the one endangering third countries by using their civilian infrastrure for military purposes.
After Libya, Zelenskyy signals wider strikes on Russian assets abroad
According to the Institute for the Study of War, the Russian corvette warship had stopped for several days in Benghazi's port to refuel and resupply.
Another Ukrainian naval drone attack on Sunday sank a Russian-owned container ship that was allegedly transporting military equipment.
Ukraine has in recent months sought to attack Russian targets further and further away, including a series of strikes in Siberia.

articles.title: Breakaway group of 110 clubs deliberately misses Football Queensland registration as revolt over $5 gate fees builds
articles.summary:
Clubs fail to sign up for 2027 season as disquiet over governing body’s executive grips football community

About 100 football clubs, representing hundreds of thousands of players, have…

blocks.text: About 100 football clubs, representing hundreds of thousands of players, have deliberately missed the deadline to sign up for next season amid a dispute with Football Queensland.
The disagreement has forced Football Australia to intervene, after a breakaway group threatened earlier this week to form its own competition.

Representatives of 110 clubs – about half of Queensland’s football clubs – attended a Tuesday night meeting to discuss the issue, a day before a deadline set by the governing body for all clubs to sign up for next season. The group includes nine of the 12 men’s national premier leagues clubs and six of the nine women’s national premier league clubs.
They unanimously agreed to not sign up.
Bardon Latrobe football club president, Gerard Doyle – whose club is part of the breakaway group – said they want to register for 2027, but won’t until their demands are met.
“The most important thing for the clubs is that we get a voice up and into Football Queensland,” he said.

“We have all signed a joint letter via a law firm. We have no confidence in the board. We have no confidence in the executive. We want to affect change, which means a change of who is running Football Queensland.”
Football Queensland hasn’t called elections for its governing board for many years, he said.
Doyle said the clubs are pushing for the central body to call elections this year. It is required by its bylaws to call elections in November, but hasn’t done so, he said.
Clubs have complained for months about what they say is a lack of transparency and governance within the body, and increasing fees with little to show for it, he said.

Some Queensland parents are made to pay $5 gate fees per person to watch their children play football. Doyle said the final straw was a proposal by Football Queensland to charge a $35 per player fee for summer competitions organised by the clubs themselves among other fee increases, a plan that has since been dropped.
“(Football Queensland) hasn’t been consultative,” he said.
“It’s simply been adding costs, adding bureaucracy, and issuing dictums down the line with no avenues for consultation or discussion”.
Clubs continue to plan to play in 2027, according to a statement posted online by the group, known as Football Clubs United.

Football Australia posted its own statement last night, saying it was “working in good faith with stakeholders towards an outcome that serves the long-term interests of the game and the communities it serves”.

It committed to facilitate “focused discussions” to resolve what is said were “unresolved issues concerning Football Queensland’s affiliation arrangements” that had “created uncertainty for players, coaches, referees, volunteers, parents and clubs across Queensland”.
“Recognising the commitment of clubs yet to affiliate to the wellbeing of their participants and the future of Queensland football, Football Australia calls on them to move to affiliation for 2027.

“For 2028, Football Queensland must publish a clear plan and timetable for reviewing ongoing arrangements with all clubs, with Football Australia participating throughout. These arrangements must be subject to meaningful and transparent consultation and agreement”.
Football Queensland has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Philippines’ Bea Millan-Windorski finishes 3rd runner-up at Miss Universe 2026
articles.summary: The 24-year-old stunner from La Union achieves the same finish as her predecessor, Ahtisa Manalo of Quezon, at Miss Universe

blocks.text: LA UNION STUNNER. Bea Millan-Windorski finishes in the top five at Miss Universe 2026.
Seven Barretto via Bea Millan-Windorski's Instagram
The 24-year-old stunner from La Union achieves the same finish as her predecessor, Ahtisa Manalo of Quezon, at Miss Universe
MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ bet Bea Millan-Windorski finished third runner-up at the 75th Miss Universe in Puerto Rico on Wednesday, November 25 (Manila time).

Puerto Rico’s Jennifer Barreto took home the title of Miss Universe 2026, and was crowned by her predecessor, Fátima Bosch of Mexico, during the coronation night at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum, San Juan.
Dominican Republic’s Melissa Núñez settled for first runner-up, while Venezuela’s Clara Vega finished second runner-up. Georgia Waddington of New Zealand secured fourth runner-up.
The 24-year-old Filipina had hoped to bring home the country’s fifth Miss Universe crown, following Catriona Gray (2018), Pia Wurtzbach (2015), Margarita Moran (1973), and Gloria Diaz (1969).

Windorski, who is of Filipino and American descent, represented La Union in Miss Universe Philippines 2026. A pageant veteran, she represented the US at Miss Earth 2024, where she was named Miss Earth-Water.

In 2024, she earned her bachelor’s degree at the University of Wisconsin-Madison College of Letters and Science, where she was able to hone in on her advocacy for Filipino heritage and environmental rights.
True to her advocacy, she focused on the environment in answering the pageant’s final question: “What does the world need most from its leaders right now?”
“As someone who has been an environmentalist my whole life, I wish that our world leaders would listen to nature and realize that we have much to learn,” Windorski said.

“I volunteered with sea turtles for the past 10 years, and while we’ve often heard of crab mentality or tearing one another down, turtle mentality is the opposite. The strongest sea turtle hatchlings actually stay behind in the nest to help their weaker brothers and sisters out and into the sea. I wish that our world leaders would embrace the same mentality.”
Windorski’s ranking comes just a year after Ahtisa Manalo of Quezon also finished third runner-up in last year’s edition. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Deal or no deal for PH? Trump’s offer on US energy, agri products
articles.summary: Philippine officials explain why Trump's buy only American farm products and energy doesn't fly

blocks.text: LEADERS. US President Donald Trump and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. talk before a bilateral meeting at the Malacanang Palace on November 18, 2026.
Rolex dela Pena/Pool via Reuters
Philippine officials explain why Trump's buy only American farm products and energy doesn't fly

items: Following the US midterms, President Trump is attempting to secure trade deals with the Philippines, claiming they will buy 100% of their energy and agriculture from the US by 2027.
Philippine officials, including Trade Secretary Cris Roque, have stated that no such agreements have been finalized and emphasized the importance of multiple trade sources for food security.
Trump's statements appear inconsistent with official White House communications, which suggest an increase in Philippine imports of US products rather than exclusive sourcing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Following the Republicans’ historic defeat in the US midterms, US President Donald Trump is now trying to cut his losses, and he’s using his engagements during the ASEAN Summit in Manila and the APEC Summit in China for this goal. (READ: [Edgewise] US midterms: After the blue tsunami, what is to be done?)

Take, for instance, his unbelievable statement on Sunday, November 22 that the Philippines will soon be buying 100% of its energy and all of its agriculture requirements from America, supposedly by January 1, 2027.

“Energy, they buy 20% from us but they buy… ‘Where do you get your energy?’ Prime Minister (sic) [Ferdinand] Marcos who’s a very good man, by the way. Great family, but I said, ‘Where do you buy your energy?’ Trump said in a press conference with the US media after the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China. “‘Sir, we buy it from the Middle East.’ I said ‘not anymore, you don’t. You’re gonna buy 100% of your energy from us.'”

Trump probably thinks the Philippines is still an American colony, and to pressure the Marcos administration into accepting this unfair deal, he uses the Philippines’ conflict with China in the West Philippine Sea as a bargaining chip.

“We support these countries [like the Philippines], but they don’t buy from us. So I said, ‘You’re going to buy 100% from — not 90, not 95…’ Is Brazil gonna help them in case they get into a little skirmish with China? I don’t think so,” Trump said.
On Tuesday, November 24, Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cris Roque said no such deals with the US have been finalized.
“We are still in the negotiating table so we cannot divulge the details,” she told Radio DzBB, citing a non-disclosure agreement that trade negotiators signed.
What she could say, however, was that such a trade deal would be unrealistic since most international trade is done by private companies, not by the government.
“What’s important for us is the world is our market and we have the option to buy from all different countries, especially [it’s the] private sector ang bumibili (who’s buying),” Roque said.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin gave a similar assurance.

“We can’t force the [fuel] companies [in the Philippines] to buy from a specific country, baka ang gobyerno pwedeng bumili ng diretso pero for stockpiling, pero it’s under negotiations e… so far, wala pa naman written na document,” Garin told Radio DzMM on Monday, November 23.
(We can’t force the companies to buy from a specific country, perhaps government can buy directly but for stockpiling, but it’s still under negotiations… so far, there’s no written document.)

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu-Laurel was quoted on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Conference on Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization on Monday that such an offer would be good for the Philippines as long as the prices of US farm produce are good, but it would not be wise in terms of food security.

“We have to have multiple sources to be food secure. Mas magandang mas marami tayong iba ibang sources, but of course kung mura naman ibebenta siguro sa atin ang agri products like soya, wheat na hindi naman finafarm, why not?” Tiu-Laurel said.

(We have to have multiple sources to be food secure. It would be better if we have various sources, but of course, if they will sell us cheaper agri products like soya, wheat which we don’t produce, why not?)

Philippine Ambassador to the US Jose Romualdez clarified that while Trump was, as usual, “straight to the point,” President Marcos was just being his “polite” self when he said he was open to the idea of complete sourcing of energy and farm products from the US.

“But the commitments will have to come when we have a complete discussion on how we will be able to achieve the proposal of President Trump. At the end of the day, the trade team, which means to say both parties have to look at the cost and how we’ll be able to get to that point,” Romualdez told One News on Monday.
“It’s a quid pro quo essentially, that’s the reality to that,” he added.

Senator Bam Aquino, in response to Senator Imee Marcos’ critical remark on the supposed deal during the Department of Trade and Industry budget hearing on Wednesday, November 25, said, “I don’t even think that’s feasible.”
Trump’s statement is also inconsistent with what the White House disclosed about the US president’s engagements with ASEAN leaders.

In the White House’s November 18 fact sheet on Trump’s “historic economic deals” from his ASEAN Summit engagements, it states: “The leaders also committed to eliminate the US trade deficit with the Philippines through increased Philippine imports of American energy and agriculture products, which will support the jobs of tens of thousands of American engineers, technicians, and farmers.”
Take note that it talks about the Philippines buying more US energy and farm products, not buying solely from America.
So, it’s really best to take Trump’s statements with a grain of salt. As the popular adage goes, “All politics is local.” – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Canada·New
Veteran sports journalist Rick Westhead's book that takes a deep dive into hockey culture in Canada has won the $70,000 Balsillie Prize for Public Policy.
We Breed Lions: Confronting Canada's Troubled Hockey Culture explores sexual assault, hazing and abuse
The Writers' Trust of Canada announced We Breed Lions: Confronting Canada's Troubled Hockey Culture as the winner of the prize at a private dinner in Toronto on Tuesday evening.
Westhead's book explores hockey's reckoning with allegations of sexual assault, hazing and abuse that rocked the sport in recent years.

articles.title: Marcos vows sustained support vs stunting under Alagang Pinas Summit
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. vowed Wednesday to sustain government programs aimed at protecting pregnant mothers and children up to two years old from stunting, as the Philippine Multisectoral…

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 12:01pm

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. vowed Wednesday to sustain government programs aimed at protecting pregnant mothers and children up to two years old from stunting, as the Philippine Multisectoral Nutrition Project (PMNP) concludes its four-year project.

“Sa pamamagitan ng Alagang Pinas Summit, ang mga serbisyon na simulan sa ilalim ng PMNP ay magpapatuloy upang ang bawat batang nangangailangan ng tulong sa nutrisyon ay makakatanggap ng angkop at sapat na pangangalaga,” Marcos said during his speech in Clark, Pampanga.
(Through the Alagang Pinas Summit, the services initiated under the PMNP will continue to ensure that every child in need of nutritional support receives appropriate and adequate care.)

The PMNP is an initiative between the Department of Health (DOH), the World Bank, and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) that aims to reduce child stunting and malnutrition by boosting access to nutrition to pregnant mothers and infants during the critical first 1,000 days.
The summit also marks the culmination of the four-year PMNP with the theme “Alagang Pinas Tungo sa Mas Malusog na Bukas: Sustained First 1,000 Days (F1KD) Convergence.”
According to Marcos, PMNP has reached 6.17 million beneficiaries in 235 participating municipalities as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Meanwhile, around 549,000 children under five benefited from the program, while 134 participating municipalities recorded significant reductions in stunting after two years.
Marcos also said the government is strengthening local implementation capacity while acknowledging existing limitations and gaps that need to be addressed.
According to DOH, the rate among children under 2 years old in the Philippines declined from 22.5% in 2023 to 21.1% in 2025.

Health Secretary Edwin Mercado had said eight out of 10 children aged 2 years old and below have adequate height for their age. The stunting rate slightly decreased from 22.5% in 2023 to 21.1% in 2025.

However, he said it is still far from the Millennium Development targets under the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition (PPAN) 2023–2028, which aims to reduce the stunting rate among children under 5 years old to 17.9% or lower by 2028.
Protect funding
In her speech, UNICEF representative in the Philippines Kyungsun Kim called for the protection of funds against stunting.
“Protect funding for nutrition year after year. Prioritizing interventions during the first 1,000 days matters,” Kim said, underscoring the importance of regularly measuring results.
“Projects have timelines, but a child's right to good health and nutrition does not,” she said.
“Keep nutrition at the heart of development plans. Make sure services reach those who need them most,” she added.
Meanwhile, Mercado pointed out the factors that need to be considered in addressing malnutrition and stunting.

“The reality is no single agency can solve malnutrition alone. It is never just a clinical issue, it is tied to clean water, early childhood care, food security, social protection, and strong local governance,” he said during the summit. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Martin Romualdez appeals 90-day suspension, says plunder allegations unclear
articles.summary: Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez has appealed the 90-day suspension imposed by the Sandiganbayan, saying it is premature amid the prosecution"s unclear P7.4 billion plunder charge.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 12:01pm
Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez has appealed the 90-day suspension imposed by the Sandiganbayan, saying it is premature amid the prosecution’s unclear P7.4 billion plunder charge.

In his motion for reconsideration, Romualdez said the Sandiganbayan did not rule on his argument that the prosecution did not identify a main plunderer, even if a 2016 Supreme Court ruling on the Arroyo v. People case requires that such should be identified when a case is filed against several individuals.

“With due respect, the [criminal] Information charges accused Romualdez and Co together with receiving the monies “by reason or on account of the respective public offices and positions of Romualdez and Co,” and with “taking undue advantage, on several occasions, of their respective official positions, authorities, relationships, connections, or influence to unjustly enrich themselves.” It does not state which of the two is the main plunderer, either does it state how much of the aggregate of P7.4 billion each of them supposedly amassed,” the former House speaker said in his appeal.

“The Questioned Resolution [imposing a suspension order] reads the Information as alleging that accused Romualdez amassed the ill-gotten wealth. The Information does not allege that accused Romualdez, as distinguished from Co, amassed it. It alleges only that Romualdez and Co enriched “themselves.” This, too, must be resolved before the Information may serve as the basis for preventive suspension,” he added.

Romualdez’s co-accused in the P7.4 billion plunder case include former House appropriations chairperson Zaldy Co of Ako Bicol party-list, Romualdez’s personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño, and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation.

“Accused Romualdez is not identified as having personally received any sum on any of the 15 occasions alleged. Neither does the [criminal information distinguish supposed receipts by an approximate date, amount, or identified transaction. A bare statement of 15 occasions, an aggregate amount, and delivery locations, do not sufficiently identify the component criminal transactions comprising the alleged series,” the lawmaker said.

Romualdez said that while the issue on whether he committed the alleged acts is a matter for trial, whether those acts have been sufficiently alleged is another question that needs to be resolved first.
“The latter must be resolved before the [criminal] information may serve as the basis for preventive suspension,” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García leaving US for Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
articles.summary: His deportation to El Salvador and return to the US became a flash point in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.

blocks.text: Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, is leaving the US for Spain.
He is set to take a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.
His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."
The BBC has contacted Ábrego García's lawyers and the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.

In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.

The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.
For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.
Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.
After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.
At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.
