articles.title: Vanity Fair's Taylor Swift exposé sparks backlash
articles.summary: The piece, which Canadian journalist May Jeong says drew from interviews with more than 100 people, rests some of its claims on anonymous accounts and memories of events from decades ago. And critics…

image.caption: A new Vanity Fair piece about Taylor Swift, pictured here in Nashville on Nov. 18, is drawing criticism for its sourcing and tone. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The piece, which Canadian journalist May Jeong says drew from interviews with more than 100 people, rests some of its claims on anonymous accounts and memories of events from decades ago. And critics have questioned what the article establishes — and what it asks readers to infer.
Critics have been taking aim at profile's claims, sources and tone
Variety Fair's The Mastermind profile offers a less-than-flattering account of Taylor Swift's relationships and public image — though it does not name the singer directly.
CBC News has contacted Jeong and Swift's representatives but did not hear back by publication time.

items: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift returns for 1st performance in 13 years

blocks.text: Claims about how Swift treats people

An anonymous music industry source identified as "The Exec" compares Swift to Regina George, the popular antagonist in 2004's Mean Girls. Another source known as "The Person Familiar" alleges that Swift "comes after you" if you disagree with her.

Toronto culture writer Stacy Lee Kong said "an anonymous source is only anonymous to the public." The journalist, fact-checker and editors would know the source’s identity, she said, as would the lawyer. While that may reassure readers that the source was checked, Lee Kong said, it doesn't prove the account is true.
Taylor Swift onstage during the 60th annual Country Music Association awards in November in Nashville. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

The profile says people close to Swift "do not dare speak ill of her — dare not speak of her at all." It cites a lawyer who chose to speak through an intermediary, a manager who asked the reporter to delete their correspondence and a pastor who said they needed the family’s permission to comment.
Lee Kong noted that people may refuse to comment or request anonymity for many reasons, including privacy or concern about professional consequences.
Disputed memories of school

Swift has spoken publicly about feeling excluded and bullied as a child. In the profile, former classmates and a teacher challenge parts of her recollections. Former classmate Chanice Skinner describes Swift as part of "the popular crowd," while music teacher Sharon Luyben disputes a story about friends moving away from Swift at lunch.

Some readers questioned the weight given to memories from decades ago. One X user wrote, "If you're coming for a 37 year old because of a bad experience you had with her in 7th grade you gotta let it go and move on."

items: Taylor Swift inducted into Songwriters Hall of Fame

blocks.text: One former classmate's recollection that Swift owned Ugg boots in three colours also became a focus of online jokes. The classmate said her single mother could not afford a pair. Critics questioned what the anecdote added to a profile making broader claims about Swift's character.
Another X user wrote, "She had three pairs of Ugg boots UGH SHES THE WORST!!! This is pathetic. 💀💀💀💀💀"

Lee Kong acknowledged that readers may want a story that feels "a bit more fair" and said she understood the criticism of the profile's emphasis on details such as the boots. At the same time, she argued that a profile of a powerful celebrity does not need to be a complete accounting of every positive and negative aspect of that person.
Feuds, nicknames and old disputes
Charli xcx, left, and Taylor Swift pose at an event at Madison Square Garden in December 2014 in New York City. (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for iHeartMedia)

The profile discusses songs by pop stars Charli xcx and Olivia Rodrigo that some fans have linked to Swift. Some listeners have interpreted Charli xcx's Sympathy is a knife as reflecting insecurity around a major pop star and Swift's Actually Romantic as a response. Rodrigo has not publicly identified the subject of the grudge.
The article also complicates the simple feud narrative, including mention of Swift praising Charli xcx's songwriting and dancing during one of Rodrigo's performances.

It also revisits Swift's dispute over the rights to her early recordings. After Big Machine Records sold the recordings to Scooter Braun's company, Swift said she had not been given the opportunity to buy them. She later re-recorded the albums.
Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce, pictured in Cleveland in May, were married in an elaborate ceremony at Madison Square Garden on July 3. (Jason Miller/Getty Images)
Wealth, wedding coverage and online reaction
Vanity Fair's account of Swift and Travis Kelce's wedding at Madison Square Garden, as well as the couple's reported donations of $26 million US, drew attention to the profile's tone.

The line "Beyond need lies want. Beyond want, greed" was especially criticized. In his column, Variety chief music critic Chris Willman called the piece a "failed exposé," while some readers said it made them more sympathetic. One X user wrote: "The Vanity Fair hit piece on Taylor Swift just made me like her even more lol."
It's official, Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce are married
The case for scrutiny

According to Lee Kong, the profile's format is "referential to Taylor Swift's work herself." It uses labels such as "The Exec" rather than names and includes hidden messages like bolded letters that refer to Swift's song Look What You Made Me Do. Still, she acknowledges that some readers may find the piece mean-spirited or ineffective.

items: Taylor Swift dropped 4 new songs. Here's what fans are sleuthing

blocks.text: Celebrity journalism can also be shaped by reporters' dependence on access, Kong said. Outlets may hesitate to criticize public figures if they worry about losing the chance to interview them.
At the same time, she argued, scrutiny still matters because celebrities can wield enormous cultural and economic influence and because fandom itself shapes public behaviour.
"I think telling the truth about people that play these really important roles actually is serious journalism."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Drops for Nvidia, Anthropic and other AI stocks drag the markets back down
articles.summary: Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower Tuesday after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled.

image.caption: eople work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, on Nov. 17. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

blocks.text: Business·New
Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower Tuesday after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled.
S&P 500 falls 0.5% to 8th loss in last 9 days

Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower Tuesday after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. That's even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with Americans' confidence in the economy.

The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent to its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks once again led the way and yanked the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.5 per cent. Stocks outside of AI held up much better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423 points, or 0.9 per cent.
In Toronto, the S&P/TSX composite index slipped 0.35 per cent.

items: Bank of Canada expects 2nd round of oil-linked inflation in 2027, Macklem says

blocks.text: They're the latest swings for a market that's been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month. The worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers' 401(k) accounts because AI companies have grown into Wall Street's most influential stocks.

While the surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO announced Monday does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it.

At the same time, high interest rates make it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry's growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres.
Tech stocks fizzle
To be sure, AI stocks and the broader U.S. market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour.
For now, at least, the momentum is back downward.
Nvidia fell 5.9 per cent day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts.
CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, tumbled 11.8 per cent. GE Vernova, which helps power AI data centres, dropped 4.8 per cent.
‘Him being reinstated does not mean being exonerated,' tech adviser says of Jensen Huang's return

And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5 per cent to drop below $83 US. That's how much it first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as $115 US in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype.

Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower, even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected.

Confidence jumped sharply for Democrats and Independents following the midterm election results, according to the Conference Board. That narrowed the wide gap between them and Republicans, whose confidence fell slightly.

The results echo a report from the University of Michigan released earlier in the month, which also showed a rise in overall sentiment following the midterm elections and a drop in oil prices from late October.
Consumer stables show strength
Companies in industries across the economy, meanwhile, continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer.

Dollar Tree climbed 11.2 per cent after reporting bigger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than they did in last year's third quarter, and more of them came in than last year.

Kohl's rallied 19.5 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected.

Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 f per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet. That's a big deal because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 36.08 points to 7,201.09. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 423.39 to 50,018.70, and the Nasdaq composite fell 356.02 to 23,733.54.
In the bond market, U.S. Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.93 per cent from 4.92 per cent late Monday after drifting up and down earlier in the day.

Oil prices rose, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil climbed 2.4 per cent to $88.78 US. It's been yo-yoing between $72 US and $114 US since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

articles.title: U.S. jury finds Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets
articles.summary: A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless…

image.caption: The signage of a Huawei office is pictured in Kanata, Ont., in May 2022. A U.S. jury has convicted the company of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
Company acquitted of most serious charge of criminal racketeering conspiracy

However, jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge typically is used in organized crime and drug cases, but prosecutors had used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from American companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which U.S. prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the U.S. and elsewhere.

Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.

Lawyers for the company said U.S. investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei's more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that didn't actually exist.
Can Canada manage the security risks that come with a China trade deal?
Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.

"That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together," and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict "repudiated the central government narrative in the case."
'Economic bullying'

It's unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei's global fortunes. The company hasn't been allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, such as Canada and Britain.

But that hasn't stopped it from doing a robust business elsewhere. Its smartphones and other telecom equipment are sold globally. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors, becoming an important alternative in China to chips made by companies such as Nvidia.

items: How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips

blocks.text: The U.S. announced its criminal charges against Huawei in early 2019 and later expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in "economic bullying" and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.
'You can't steal a secret that isn't a secret'

The indictment against Huawei accused it of a long pattern of outright technology thefts. Huawei, prosecutors said, once sold internet routers containing source code copied from a competitor. In another episode, a person working for Huawei slipped into a competitor's booth at a Chicago trade show to surreptitiously photograph the circuits inside another company's networking device, the indictment said.
Prosecutors said that on another occasion, a Huawei worker removed a robotic arm from a competitor's lab so it could be photographed and measured.
The victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu, according to court records.

"The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct, like lying to Congress, lying to banks, violating U.S. sanctions and trying to interfere with the very criminal investigation that led to this case," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told the jury at the trial.

items: Big tech getting glimpse at espionage threats, which extend beyond sector

blocks.text: In his closing argument to jurors, Huawei's lawyer said prosecutors leaned on "innuendo and facts ripped out of context," and testimony from ex-employees "with a bone to pick," to pursue a company that had relied on "hard work, innovation and competition" to succeed.
"Huawei didn't steal its way to success," Heberlig said, noting that much of the material the U.S. alleges was stolen was already public.
"You can't steal a secret that isn't a secret," he said.

He said Huawei paid billions of dollars in licensing fees over the years, with 75 per cent of that money going to U.S. companies, and had reprimanded or fired employees found to have engaged in wrongdoing.

Heberlig noted that lines of Cisco source code turned up in Huawei software more than two decades ago. He said when the source-code copying was discovered, Huawei recalled routers sold in the U.S. and offered to replace them with Cisco routers and created a "compliance culture that permeates Huawei today."
Meng Wanzhou, chief financial officer of Huawei, reads a statement outside B.C. Supreme Court, in Vancouver, in September 2021. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

U.S. prosecutors had originally also brought criminal charges against Huawei's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, accusing her of misleading HSBC bank about the company's business dealings in Iran.

Meng, the daughter of Huawei's founder, was arrested in Canada in 2018, but ultimately was allowed to return to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China. As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its case against her.
The trial in New York overlapped with a summit meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin in the technology-centric city of Shenzhen, China.

articles.title: Stellantis taking Unifor to court over obstruction of environmental work
articles.summary: The ongoing dispute over the sale of Stellantis' Brampton, Ont., assembly plant is heading to court, as the automaker has filed a lawsuit alleging Unifor is impeding an environmental assessment…

image.caption: In documents filed in an Ontario court last Thursday, Stellantis said it is seeking an injunction requiring the union, its national president and Unifor Local 1285's plant chair to refrain from blocking the Brampton plant and preventing work at the site. (Arlyn McAdorey/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

The ongoing dispute over the sale of Stellantis' Brampton, Ont., assembly plant is heading to court, as the automaker has filed a lawsuit alleging Unifor is impeding an environmental assessment necessary to the transaction.
Documents filed in Ontario Superior Court of Justice last Thursday, Stellantis seeking injunction
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 24, 2026 4:03 PM EST | Last Updated: 27 minutes ago

In documents filed last Thursday in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Stellantis said it is seeking an injunction requiring the union, its national president Lana Payne and Unifor Local 1285 plant chair Ardis Snow to refrain from blocking the Brampton plant and preventing work at the site.

The company wants the court to declare that the union has trespassed at the facility and "obstructed the lawful entrance to and exit from the premises," which has restricted Stellantis’ ability to provide access to environmental consulting firm Pinchin Ltd.

A statement of claim says Pinchin was retained by Roshel — the armoured vehicle manufacturer that agreed to buy the idled Brampton plant from Stellantis — to carry out environmental work starting Nov. 9. The allegations have not yet been tested in court.

However, Stellantis says that morning, union representatives blockaded entrances to the plant with trucks, pylons and individuals carrying Unifor flags and that Unifor told the automaker it wouldn't let Pinchin personnel or equipment through.
Unifor national president Lana Payne says in a statement that the union "has been demonstrating in support of Canadian jobs at the Brampton plant throughout the past year."
"We continue to fight for the jobs of our members and for the entire Canadian auto industry," Payne said.
"The sale of the plant to Roshel is unacceptable to our union. And we will continue to work with all parties to try to get a different outcome.”

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
articles.summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.

blocks.text: Huawei has been guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US, AP reports.
In the two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".

articles.title: Australian politics live: Chalmers notes ‘serious moment for our economy’; inflation expected to jump to 4.8%
articles.summary: • Get our daily political email, free app or

blocks.text: Chalmers notes ‘serious moment for our economy’ but downplays recession fears

blocks.caption: Caitlin Cassidy

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has downplayed any fears of an incoming recession while acknowledging it is a “very serious time” for Australia’s economy.

This week, Chalmers presented a special economic statement warning unemployment would climb above 5% alongside slower economic growth for the next two years. He flagged modest cuts in next month’s mid-year budget update, including to the public service.
Chalmers told the ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening that it had been a “very difficult year” for Australians, which had been reflected in the polls and political commentary:

double quotation markI take responsibility for the fact that we’re pushing hard reforms through the parliament at the same time as people are under pressure … But I’m not focused on the commentary or the columns in the newspapers. I’m focused on doing the right thing for the right reasons. Not just acknowledging the pressures that people are under, but taking responsibility for responding to them.
Chalmers maintained neither the treasury or reserve bank were forecasting a recession or “expecting our economy to go backwards”, but added:
double quotation markThere are risks and pressures and challenges all around our domestic economy and indeed right around the global economy. This is a very serious moment for our economy.
Key events

items: 1h agoChalmers notes ‘serious moment for our economy’ but downplays recession fears
1h agoSolomon Islands to end China security pact, sign new Australia treaty

blocks.text: Wells says meeting with US ambassador ‘really useful’
Anika Wells says she won’t hypothesise what the United States will do, if anything, after the US ambassador raised “objections” to the digital duty of care bill.
As my colleague, Josh Butler, wrote below, the ambassador said vaguely defined harms and penalties will “push platforms to censor lawful speech”.
Wells, speaking to RN Breakfast, says as she did yesterday that the two have spoken and that they’re “ironing out” differences of opinion.

double quotation markIt’s not for me to hypothesise what another nations administration might want to do. I did meet with ambassador [David] Brat yesterday morning. It was our first meeting together. It was really useful. I think we both understand each other’s positions and we’re ironing out where there are points of difference. Like I said, we won’t take a backward step from protecting Australian kids and helping Australian parents, and they won’t take a backward step from their position.

blocks.caption: Josh Butler

blocks.text: Josh Butler
US ambassador criticises Labor’s digital duty of care bill
The American ambassador to Australia has raised “objections” to Labor’s digital duty of care bill, saying he was “concerned” it would hurt US tech businesses.

“Vaguely defined “harms” backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” David Brat wrote on social media, after a meeting with communications minister Anika Wells.

The bill has not yet passed, but is in the final stages of Senate processes. Wells said she met Brat yesterday, with US tech companies some of the most prominent to be captured by the laws; Wells has previously said Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform would be subject to the laws but that the government had committed to “constructive dialogue” with the US, including during her Tuesday meeting with Brat.
“I think we would say there are points of differences, and we’re ironing them out,” Wells said of her meeting with Brat.
But the US ambassador, posting a photo of that meeting - where both were smiling - wrote online that “free speech is the foundation of a free society, and protecting it is a U.S. priority.”

double quotation markToday I met Minister for Communications Anika Wells and laid out the Trump Administration’s well-known objections to the Digital Duty of Care Legislation. Vaguely defined “harms,” backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech. As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the U.S. is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.
‘On the road to economic ruin’ the new Coalition catch phrase
The Coalition is sharpening its lines and slogans, and trying to get itself into shape for an election as early as next year.
Its smelling blood in the water with Labor and the prime minister’s support sinking.
Angus Taylor, speaking to journalists in the press gallery corridor is keen to use the phrase that the country under Labor is “on the road to economic ruin”.
In five minutes, he uses it four times.

double quotation markI tell you what’s down though, real wages, incomes, our standard of living, the biggest collapse. The biggest collapse of any developed country in the world. And we’ve got inflation data out today, the expectation is it will be high again. I think the country is on the road to economic ruin.
Coalition welcomes Solomon Islands dropping China pact
Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, has welcomed Solomon Islands scrapping its pact with Beijing and signing a treaty with Australia – with the leader, Matthew Wale, in Canberra today.
The landmark agreement, signed between Honiara and Beijing in 2022, will not be renewed after the five-year deal expires in April next year.

It was signed in the weeks leading up to the 2022 federal election under the then Morrison government, which Penny Wong called Australia’s “worst foreign policy blunder in the Pacific since the end of World War II”.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Taylor is asked how a Coalition government would stop that happening again. Taylor says the problem was actually Solomon Islands’ leadership at the time:

double quotation markWell, you do have to nurture these relationships. It’s important. Obviously, it depends on who’s leading, and we have a leader there now who is determined to drop that arrangement. And that is a good thing. We welcome it very much.

blocks.caption: Angus Taylor. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

blocks.text: Good morning
Krishani Dhanji here with you for the second-last sitting day of the year.

(The sitting week technically ends tomorrow, but if the government secures an 11th-hour deal on its key bills, it could end up passing them with amendments in the Senate late Thursday and recalling the lower house on Friday.)

As we reported earlier, Solomon Islands’ prime minister, Matthew Wale, is in town today to sign a new treaty with Australia, after it was revealed the Pacific nation would end its security pact with China. Even the opposition was positive about the deal, with Andrew Hastie crediting the government with the “win”.
Inflation data will come out today, something we (and the rest of the country) have been laser focused on, and is likely to be less of a win for Labor. We’ll bring you all the reaction to that too.
I’ve got my coffee, I hope you’ve got yours – let’s get stuck in!

blocks.caption: Patrick Commins

blocks.text: Patrick Commins
Inflation expected to jump when latest figures released today
The government’s economic management will be back in the spotlight today, with official figures at 11.30am expected to show inflation jumping to 4.8% in the year to October.
That’s well up on the 4.3% annual rate in September, and will be nearly double the Reserve Bank’s official target of 2.5%.
Once again, it’s rising fuel costs that are driving the headline inflation number in the wrong direction.
Nab’s economists reckon fuel costs will contribute 1.2 percentage points to annual inflation, which they predict will be 4.7% (so slightly below the consensus forecast).
The ban of card surcharges from 1 October will also add a bit to price pressures, although how much is unclear.

Only 16% of firms charged surcharges, but there was evidence that the introduction of the ban was used by a wider range of businesses as an excuse to pass on other cost increases to their customers through higher prices.

The RBA will be focused on what is happening to underlying price pressures. The so-called “trimmed mean” inflation measure, which removes the most volatile prices, is expected to bump up to 3.7%, from 3.6%, according to the consensus forecast.
The better news is that analysts believe this should mark a high-water mark for inflation.

“An outcome in line with our forecast would be no comfort to the RBA, but we expect October to mark the peak for headline inflation and to overstate the underlying momentum in trimmed mean,” NAB said.
The best evidence of this is that financial markets are pricing in rate cuts next year.
Solomon Islands to end China security pact, sign new Australia treaty

blocks.caption: Tess Ikonomou

blocks.text: Tess Ikonomou
Solomon Islands will end its contentious security pact with China, in a major diplomatic win for Australia.
Guardian Australia has confirmed the landmark agreement, signed between Honiara and Beijing in 2022, will not be renewed after the five-year deal expires in April next year.
In a statement, the Solomon Islands government confirmed its prime minister, Matthew Wale, will travel to Canberra to sign a treaty with Australia on Wednesday, reported to be worth almost $1bn.
To keep China at bay in the Pacific, the Albanese government has since inked a number of security agreements, including mutual-defence pacts with Fiji and Papua New Guinea.

blocks.caption: Solomon Islands prime minister Matthew Wale at Cop31 in Turkey. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

blocks.text: Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
articles.summary: The Emir of Daura is one of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, with politicians often trying to gain his support.

blocks.text: One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.
The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.
The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.
Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.
Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.
On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.
She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.
After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.
According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.
The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.
It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.
However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.
The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

articles.title: Minister defends 2027 permanent residency plan, says 'vast majority' are already in Canada
articles.summary: Immigration Minister Lena Diab says the federal government is managing newcomers responsibly as the Conservative Opposition seeks to block a plan that could see as many as 662,000 people receive…

image.caption: Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Lena Metlege Diab says a one-time measure will add a maximum of 200,000 permanent residents above federal targets. Her office said most of those people are already in Canada. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Immigration Minister Lena Diab says the federal government is managing newcomers responsibly as the Conservative Opposition seeks to block a plan that could see as many as 662,000 people receive permanent residency next year.
Conservative motion seeks to block government's plan
Ottawa has an annual target of 380,000 permanent resident admissions for the next three years. But up to 282,000 additional permanent admissions are planned through one-time measures in 2027.
Diab's office says the "vast majority of these admissions will be transitioning people who are already in Canada to permanent residence."
As part of that total, Diab says 100,000 slots are for workers who will be nominated by provinces and territories, and those slots will go unfilled if those governments decide they don't need them.

items: Carney says new immigration levels plan is 'sustainable' as it draws ire of Conservatives
Conservatives accuse government of 'cooking the books' over immigration data presentation

blocks.text: Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argues Canada can't absorb all of those people without putting additional strains on the housing and job markets and social infrastructure.
An Opposition motion being debated on Parliament Hill on Tuesday calls to block the government's permanent residency plan
The Bloc Québécois says it plans to support the Conservative motion, which cannot pass without the support of some members of the Liberal majority government.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: Life expectancy in Cuba falls for first time since 1950 amid economic crisis
articles.summary:
WHO chief says life expectancy has fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 in 2025, figures that predate US fuel blockade

Life expectancy has fallen for the first time in Cuba since 1950 as…

blocks.text: Life expectancy has fallen for the first time in Cuba since 1950 as the island reels from a severe economic crisis, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday.
On a visit to Havana, WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said life expectancy had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025, the first decline since records began in 1950.
The 2025 figures predate the US imposition of a crippling fuel blockade on the communist-run island in January.
The blockade, which builds on a six-decade US trade embargo, sharply accelerated the worst crisis in Cuba in decades, leaving state services on the brink of collapse.
At a press conference, Tedros painted a grim picture of a health system in “critical” condition.
He said the infant mortality rate had more than doubled, from approximately four deaths per 1,000 live births in 2020 to 9.9 in 2025.
Maternal mortality increased from 37.4 per 1,000 live births in 2019 to 44.1 last year.
Meanwhile, the survival rate for childhood cancer has decreased from 85% to 65% since January, when Washington threatened sanctions on any country supplying fuel to Cuba.
Tedros announced $2m in aid for childhood vaccination programs and the purchase of essential medical equipment.
He linked the health situation in Cuba to the “sanctions” but also referred to “internal problems” and said it was “positive” that Cuba was addressing them.
He was referring to Cuba’s announcement of wide-ranging market-led economic reforms.
“The reform the government is proposing concerns the economy, the market, health, almost every sector. And we support it,” Tedros said.

articles.title: Armed men take 25 hostages at supermarket in one of Colombia’s top tourist destinations
articles.summary:
Police say group seized store in city of Cartagena and local media showed footage of snipers on nearby buildings

A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the

blocks.text: A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding 25 people hostage, the president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said on Tuesday.
De la Espriella, said the men were “common criminals” who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
Military and police forces have been deployed to the hostage site, Colombian police said.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have shown footage of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.

“Thirty people were kidnapped, five ​of whom have already been released. They are older women,” said de la Espriella from the city of ​Villavicencio, where he traveled after an overnight bombing ​there.

Cartagena is one of Colombia’s main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.

The Rafael Núñez airport in Cartagena temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday after the incident, as the armed forces used one of the runways in ​connection with ​the incident. It later said operations were slowly returning to normal and landings were reopened about 45 minutes after the suspension.
Local media reported the hostages are ​being her at the Castellana location of ​the ⁠Éxito supermarket chain.
More details soon …

articles.title: Bank of Canada expects 2nd round of oil-linked inflation in 2027, Macklem says
articles.summary: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem sees high energy prices continuing to sting consumers at the fuel pump and beyond in 2027, even as oil prices fall from recent peaks.

image.caption: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem, seen here in Ottawa on Oct. 28, said Tuesday that oil shock linked to the war in the Middle East will stoke inflation again next year. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem sees high energy prices continuing to sting consumers at the fuel pump and beyond in 2027, even as oil prices fall from recent peaks.
Says central bank is bracing for 'larger and more frequent supply shocks'

In a speech on Tuesday, he warned a second round of the recent oil shock linked to war in the Middle East will stoke inflation next year. His remarks dampen expectations that a recent decline in benchmark oil prices would yield meaningful relief for consumers and businesses.
"This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence," he said at an event hosted by the Economic Club of Canada, in Toronto on Tuesday.
"Historical lags and our own business surveys suggest more pass-through to the consumer in the year ahead."
Macklem added that so far, businesses have largely absorbed higher production and transportation costs linked to high energy prices.

The October inflation data from Statistics Canada gave little evidence of high oil prices spilling into other segments of the economy. The consumer price index rose 3.1 per cent on a year-over-year basis last month, matching a 3.1 per cent increase in September.
Last month, the Bank of Canada hiked its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, ending a year-long pause at 2.25 per cent with its first increase since 2023.
Tiff Macklem on what might prompt another rate hike

In their summary of deliberations published on Nov. 10, policymakers said further hikes may be needed as high oil prices and rising business costs collide with a resilient economy, risking broad-based inflation through 2027.

In its October Monetary Policy Report, the Bank of Canada called for inflation to remain near three per cent through much of 2027. At the time, policymakers said they expect prices to ease toward two per cent, the mid-point of the central bank's target range, in 2028.

Since then, global oil benchmarks have fallen to roughly three-month lows, due in part to potential military de-escalation between the United States and Iran. The situation has been helped by rising exports of Middle Eastern oil to global markets through the Strait of Hormuz, the vital shipping route that’s been heavily disrupted by the conflict.
Looking ahead, Mackelm said the Bank of Canada is preparing to respond to "larger and more frequent supply shocks."
"Inflation is likely to be pushed off course more frequently and for longer," he said on Tuesday.

items: Macklem to step down in 2027

blocks.text: "Monetary policy can’t lower global energy prices. But it can limit how much they spill over. Our goal is to avoid a situation where Canadians face rising prices for a wide range of goods and services."
The Bank of Canada is scheduled to make its final rate decision of 2026 on Dec. 9.

Its governing council will have two fresh economic data points to consider ahead of that meeting. Statistics Canada is scheduled to release its gross domestic product reading for the third quarter on Nov. 30, followed by the November Labour Force Survey on Dec. 4.

Tuesday’s speech is one of Macklem's first major public appearances since announcing earlier this month that he will not seek a second term, and will step down when his seven-year mandate expires on June 2.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: Israel attempts to jail Palestinian student at Hebrew University without trial
articles.summary:
Mahdi Tounsi appeared to have suffered maltreatment at hearing where he was not allowed to hear prosecution case against him

Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court hearing in Jerusalem, as academics and activists warned that Israel’s attempt to jail him without trial marked a serious escalation in attacks on Palestinian rights.
Yael Berda, a lawyer and sociology professor at Hebrew University, who has taught Tounsi for four years, came to court to call for his release.

“I have no doubt this is a case of political persecution based on identity and political activity,” she said outside the courtroom. “Mehdi’s arrest is part of a campaign that we’ve seen very much escalating since the elections.”
Her student was “almost unrecognisable” when he appeared on a video link in the courtroom, deprived of his glasses, with his hair and beard shaved and with visible bruising, she added.

blocks.caption: Mahdi Tounsi appears at the hearing via video link. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Tounsi, a sociology and criminology student at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, was seized from his dorm on 8 November. He is held at Megiddo prison where documented abuse includes starvation rations, violent attacks on prisoners and rampant scabies and other diseases.

Thousands of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank are held under administrative detention orders but they have rarely been used against Palestinians who have Israeli citizenship or residence status in occupied East Jerusalem.
Prison authorities had not complied with a judge’s order to return Tounsi’s glasses, his brief public appearance on Tuesday showed.
Israeli prosecutors are seeking an administrative detention order, which allows for up to six months’ detention without trial or public presentation of evidence.
Security forces presented a summary of evidence in a hearing closed even to Tounsi and his lawyers, making a defence effectively impossible.

Tounsi’s arrest comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.

Noa Dagoni, executive director of Jerusalem-focused rights group Ir Amin, described Tounsi’s arrest as a dangerous escalation in political persecution of activists, particularly those “at the junction of human rights, dialogue and non-violent action”.

Many of the Ir Amin staff count Tounsi as a personal friend after years working together in his home community of Silwan, where Israeli authorities are forcing mass displacements of Palestinians, including to make way for a theme park.

Dagoni fears he may have been targeted for this work. “We’re very concerned that this [arrest] has to do with his being a non-violent peace activist, also dealing with the displacement in his community,” she said.
“The partnership of Israelis and Palestinians is very intimidating for this government because it can be effective, it can build real political power.”
Officers from the Shin Bet security force failed to appear in court to present evidence at a first hearing last week, so the judge reconvened on Tuesday.

Reflecting concern about the case, his family and lawyer were joined in the courthouse by prominent activists, Knesset member Ofer Cassif, diplomats from Ireland, the Netherlands and the EU, his tutor and the dean of students from Hebrew University.
Hundreds of Jewish and Palestinian demonstrators gathered in the street outside calling for his immediate release.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators outside the district court in Jerusalem on 24 November campaigning against the administrative detention of Mahdi Tounsi.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Many knew Tounsi personally from classes or activism, including Lana, a Palestinian citizen of Israel.

“Someone who I know being kidnapped was really frightening,” she said. “It makes me think of my place here also, how it might affect me and if there are more people who I know who are going to be arrested soon.”

Many protesters were angry with university authorities, including Arielle, 27, a former student at the same campus. “Israeli universities need to take accountability for this, like they can’t allow students to be kidnapped from their dorm rooms,” she said.

Hebrew University’s dean of students, Zohar Kampf, said the university asked to testify but its request was rejected. The university has not commented on Tounsi’s violent arrest, deprivation of glasses and other mistreatment.

Cassif, the Knesset member, called for a global pressure campaign. “Where is the international community, especially academia. What are they waiting for?” he said. “Speak up, do something, raise your voice.”

The police did not respond to questions about visible marks of abuse or details of the case against Tounsi. A spokesperson said: “The suspect was lawfully arrested as part of an investigation conducted by the Jerusalem District Central Investigations Unit concerning ties to an act of terrorism.”

articles.title: European court finds states can turn back migrants in some cases
articles.summary: Europe's top human rights court ruled that member states can turn back migrants unless they've been identified as people who were at risk of suffering or ill-treatment.

image.caption: People in this particular case said their rights were violated and that they had been turned back to Belarus even though they were vulnerable to ill-treatment [FILE: Poland/Belarus border, 2021]Image: Policja Podlaska/REUTERS

blocks.text: The European Court of Human Rights on Tuesday ruled that states belonging to the Council of Europe group have a right to control foreign arrivals.

But the court ruling said all 46 member states of the group — that includes all EU and some non-EU countries and promotes democracy and human rights on the continent — must ensure and uphold human rights of people even in hostile environments.

The European court ruling is a complicated one since it deals with a case concerning the entry of nationals of Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba into EU member countries Poland, Latvia and Lithuania between 2021 and 2022.

That was a time when a border standoff was playing out between Belarus and the EU's eastern member states, with Belarus having been accused of entirely manufacturing a migration crisis to put pressure on the EU.
Belarus arranged for people from various third countries to enter their state and then pointed them to the EU's frontiers.
Europe's human rights court says countries can turn back migrants with duty of care
Europe's most important human rights court on Tuesday ruled that states have a right to control the entry of foreign nationals into their territory even when migration has been weaponized.
The court calls Belarus' hostile actions of 2021 as having been an instance of "instrumentalization of migration."
But the court said that states must still ensure that migrants are protected against inhumane or degrading treatment.
In the context of a surge in migration, for example, national authorities were still to identify people who were particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill treatment.

The migrants in the case brought before the European court said that they had been violently prevented from crossing into the EU without their asylum applications having been examined and that their human rights had been violated.

"In a context of instrumentalization of migration, the removal of a foreign national to the instrumentalizing state would not, as such, constitute a violation of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman and degrading treatment)," the court press release said.
The court ordered Poland, Latvia and Lithuania to pay compensation for their treatment of migrants at the EU's external borders with Belarus.
Five EU countries announce plan with Rwanda to establish 'return hub'
Five EU countries also last week announced a plan with Rwanda to establish a so-called return hub in the African nation.
The hub will host rejected asylum seekers waiting to return to their countries of origin.
But there are many concerns about the project since Rwanda ranks low on human rights measures and there are questions about whether people's rights will be sufficiently protected.

articles.title: Nvidia shares slide as Trump's role in Jensen Huang's comeback questioned by US politicians
articles.summary: Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, but some of the gains reversed in Tuesday trading.

blocks.text: Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang was handed back his job at the AI microchip maker on Monday less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
Trump has said he played a big role in the 63-year-old's reinstatment, which has led to questions and backlash from US lawmakers.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down almost 8% on Tuesday, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's shock return was revealed.
However, Nvidia was not the only semiconductor chip company to experience share price declines on Tuesday, with rival AMD down more than 10%.

Broadcom and Marvell Technology shares were also lower, suggesting that investors were continuing to weigh up concerns over potential regulation by newly-elected Democrats, as well as the central question as to whether the huge amounts being invested in AI will pay off.
Nvidia's share price for example, is down almost 30% over the past six months and had been on the decline before the scandal involving its co-founder emerged earlier this month.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump told CNBC. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.

Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

articles.title: Alberta premier, justice minister to introduce Sovereignty Act motion
articles.summary: The Alberta government says it plans to introduce a new motion under its Sovereignty Act on Tuesday.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to the media in Calgary, Alta., Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Smith and Justice Minister Mickey Amery are set to introduce a motion under the province's Sovereignty Act on Tuesday. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
The Alberta government says it plans to introduce a new motion under its Sovereignty Act on Tuesday.
Proposal intended to 'defend Albertans’ fundamental rights and freedoms'
A news release says Premier Danielle Smith and Justice Minister Mickey Amery will introduce a motion "to defend Albertans’ fundamental rights and freedoms."
The news conference starts at noon in Edmonton. You can watch it here.

The UCP government passed the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act in 2022. It allows the province to push back on federal laws or policies that the legislature deems unconstitutional, violate Albertans' rights or negatively impact the province.
Last year, the province introduced a Sovereignty Act motion against federal firearms legislation.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Trevor Howlett is a journalist with CBC Edmonton. He previously reported in Nova Scotia, Fort McMurray and Red Deer. You can reach him at trevor.howlett@cbc.ca.

articles.title: French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
articles.summary: It is the latest case involving Nicolas Sarkozy who became the first French ex-president to go to jail last year.

blocks.text: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.
The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.
The pair deny any wrongdoing.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.
Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.
In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.
Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face the charge of "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised group and receiving stolen goods related to witness tampering". They deny any wrongdoing.

articles.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy and Hungary's Magyar meet amid thaw in ties
articles.summary: Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar has arrived in Ukraine for meetings with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and ethnic Hungarians. Both leaders say they want better relations after a change of…

image.caption: The tone between Budapest and Kyiv changed considerably after Hungarians elected Peter Magyar (right) to replace long-serving pro-Russian PM Viktor Orban [FILE: October 2026]Image: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hungary's new Prime Minister Peter Magyar arrived in Ukraine on Tuesday afternoon for meetings with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as well as with ethnic Hungarians living in the west of the country.

The meeting comes as both say they want better relations after a change of leadership in Budapest — no doubt a welcome change for Kyiv after years of Viktor Orban obstructing funding for its self-defense against full-scaler Russian invasion.

Ukraine's Zelenskyy posted his thanks for the meeting with a photo on X, writing: "A visit that is sure to bring positive results. We already have agreements in the areas of politics, energy, and infrastructure. Thank you!"
Despite his softer approach, Magyar has said Hungary will not be sending arms to Kyiv while at the same time vowing, "we stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."
Rights of ethnic Hungarians tied to war support and EU accession talks

Magyar has insisted that the rights of tens of thousands of ethnic Hungarians in the Transcarpathia — a region that was part of Austria-Hungary until the end of World War I and situated at the borders of Ukraine, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia — be resolved before Budapest can wholeheartedly back Ukraine and its possible accession to the European Union.

Relations deteriorated significantly over the issue in 2017, when Kyiv passed a law making Ukrainian the official language of all secondary education in Ukraine, something Budapest viewed as discriminatory toward ethnic Hungarians.

Last month, Ukrainian lawmakers passed legislation allowing ethnic minorities in the country expanded rights regarding the teaching and use of their native languages. The move was welcomed by Budapest and Hungary dropped its opposition to Brussels opening accession talks with Ukraine.
Magyar pitched this week's trip — the first to Transcarpathia by a Hungarian prime minister since 2015 — in April, after defeating Orban.

Before departing for Ukraine, the Hungarian leader said: "I hope these talks will be successful. I think this is a historic day and a good opportunity to put Ukrainian-Hungarian relations on a new footing and to rebuild trust as we did with our other neighbors."

articles.title: NPC: 11 gov't agencies yet to fully explain data breaches
articles.summary: The National Privacy Commission (NPC) said that 11 government agencies have yet to submit a full breach report following hacking incidents.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 12:24am
The National Privacy Commission (NPC) said that 11 government agencies have yet to submit a full breach report following hacking incidents.
NPC spokesperson Jose Amelito Belarmino II said that a total of 13 government agencies were reportedly hacked.

“Inaantay namin iyong full breach report ng ilang ahensiya. In fact, doon sa 13 na government agencies na na-breach at nag-report sa amin noong between November 9 to November 13, dalawa pa lamang iyong nagsusumite ng full breach report. So iyong iba po, wala pa pong isinusumite,” Belarmino said on the Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon public briefing on Tuesday,

(We are waiting for the full breach report from several agencies. In fact, from the 13 government agencies that were breached from November 9 to 13, only two submitted their full breach report. The others have not submitted.)
The Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) were the two that reportedly already submitted, but Belarmino did not name the other 11.
In addition to the 13 agencies, the Department of Migrant Workers was also hacked. It must also submit a report.
Belarmino said that under the law, agencies that were hacked are required to submit a full report five days after they notify the NPC.
Failure to submit the full breach report was already a violation, said Belarmino. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling for the rapid acceptance of his country into NATO. However, the necessary unanimity for this is lacking, as shown during the NATO Parliamentary…

image.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy participated in the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video conferenceImage: Liesa Johannssen/REUTERS

blocks.text: It took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.

"Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this."
Western allies boost Ukraine's defenses but clash over deep strikes
Ukraine seeks to join NATO

Zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That issue is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.

After the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?"

There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members currently lack unanimity on this issue. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte said.
If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared?
Merz: Denying Ukraine NATO membership in 2008 'was a mistake'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz said at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.

Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these issues might come up again."

The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he said weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply."
Why Germany's military ambitions face a battle at home
Germany's military budget has had a massive increase

The contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).

The Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer said. Also, a much larger one than before. "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness."

Following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who showed keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's new post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Irish plan offers Burnham breakthrough on Made in Europe
articles.summary: Irish presidency of EU proposes giving UK ‘partner’ status on assembly of cars in possible boost to reset of relations

blocks.text: The UK wwould not have to follow the EU and apply tariffs on Chinese car imports under an Irish proposal that could prove another breakthrough for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, in his reset of relations with the bloc.

Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency and plays a central role in steering legislation, has come up with a compromise under which the UK would be included in the bloc’s new “Made in Europe” legislation without having to align with the EU’s trade policies.

Made in Europe, or the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is designed to protect the bloc’s supply chains from cheap competition, mainly from China, particularly in the automotive and clean energy sectors.

It is understood that in a fourth compromise text, due to be considered by EU competition ministers on 3 December, Ireland has proposed giving the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK “partner” status for the assembly of cars.
This would allow not only cars such as the Mini, made at BMW’s Oxford factory, to qualify as European, but also vehicles made by the Japanese firm Nissan at its vast Sunderland plant.
Under the compromise, a “partner” country would agree to mutual access to any subsidies available to EU-owned assembly plants, and to public procurement contracts for fleet cars.

Irish negotiators have also suggested giving Japan and South Korea, which lobbied hard against the original Made in Europe proposals, access to public procurement and other public support schemes for car parts and components.

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said: “Having listened closely to all member states, the presidency has proposed a pragmatic and balanced way forward on the IAA to deliver for European competitiveness.”
Burnham last week took the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people.
The latest iteration of the IAA text is designed to reflect the car sector’s position as a cornerstone of European industry.

France, which championed the legislation, originally opposed the inclusion of the UK at all but dropped its opposition last month on condition that the UK dynamically align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles.

But this caused further tensions with the UK. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, insisted the British government would not be coerced into imposing tariffs on Chinese vehicles and would only take steps that were in the national interest.

Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said the UK “should not become collateral damage” from measures intended to address concerns arising elsewhere in the global market.
The UK car industry has argued that it is so intertwined with its EU counterparts that both sides would be damaged if the UK was not included in Made in Europe.
after newsletter promotion
Hawes said: “It is essential that the final arrangements recognise the unique UK-EU automotive relationship as allies in adversity, and do not create new barriers to our shared supply chains.”
The latest proposal will be discussed by an EU working group involving industry leaders and EU member states on Friday, before being finessed further for consideration by ministers.

European carmakers are attempting to respond to a flood of cheap Chinese electric vehicles into the bloc. ⁠Volkswagen began wage talks ⁠with labour representatives on ​Tuesday amid mounting worker anger over deep cost cuts, with protesters carrying black coffins to symbolise what they said was the death of trust and the company’s future prospects.

blocks.caption: Coffins at a Volkswagen protest in Emden, Germany, on Tuesday. Photograph: Leon Kuegeler/Reuters

blocks.text: China faces further restrictions on its trade with EU: tariffs were imposed on Chinese EV imports in 2024, and quotas agreed with Beijing in October come into force on 1 December.

The Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD ⁠said on ⁠Tuesday that it had entered into exclusive ⁠negotiations with the billionaire Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Automotive to buy ⁠its manufacturing plant in ‌Hambach, France, ‌as it seeks ‌more European production ahead of Made in Europe legislation expected next year.
Separately, Ineos said on Tuesday it would begin production of its Grenadier 4x4 in the US in 2028.

articles.title: HIV infections could rise amid aid cuts, UN warns
articles.summary: The impact of United States government funding cuts has been dramatic for many HIV programs, UNAIDS warned. The agency expects that 2027 data to show an increase in new infections after being on the…

image.caption: US contributions for HIV programs have dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025 [FILE: February 2025]Image: MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.

"The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency said in its annual global update.

AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades. According to the organization, this was made possible by broader access to treatment and improvements in the quality of care programs.
The virus claimed roughly 570,000 lives globally in 2025. This means almost 1,600 people died everyday. In comparison, this figure was 600,000 in 2024 and 1.3 million in 2010.
Based on data from 172 countries, the agency estimated that 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2025, of whom 32.1 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment.

The wider use of antiretroviral medication also reduces the risk of HIV transmission, the organization said. It estimates that 1.2 million people contracted HIV in 2025, down from 1.3 million the year before. The peak in 1994 saw 3.5 million.

blocks.caption: UNAIDS said Lenacapavir, an injection administered just twice a year, has marked another turning point in HIV prevention [FILE: July 2024]Image: Nardus Engelbrecht/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: "HIV, which was once a death sentence, has become a manageable health condition for millions of people thanks to life-saving HIV medicines," said UNAIDS.
'Dramatic impacts' of US aid cuts
Despite the encouraging data so far, cuts to international funding have hampered efforts to fight HIV, the agency warned.
HIV programs faced an 18-percent decrease in international financing over the past year, said UNAIDS.
"Funding losses have destabilized HIV programs worldwide, coinciding with a wider contraction in official development assistance over the years," it said.
Although the United States remains the largest international donor for HIV programs, its contributions dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025.
How USAID cuts could result in higher HIV transmission
After dismantling USAID, the world's largest foreign aid agency, last year, the Donald Trump administration has sought to replace decades of aid with new bilateral deals.
"The impact of the United States government funding cuts has been especially dramatic given the reliance of many countries on its support for core HIV programs," said UNAIDS.
Meanwhile disbursements from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria dropped by 13% in 2025.
Next year's data may show rising infections

"We are on the cusp of ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global ​health – and just when we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights is ​threatening to take away our gains," Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told ​Reuters.
"We haven't ‌got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs of reversals," she added.
Byanyima predicted that data released in 2027 would begin to reflect a rise in new HIV infections.
In 2015, the UN set a goal to end AIDS by 2030.
