articles.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
articles.summary:
Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran

Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other Southeast Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency.
“It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.”
Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Trump’s behaviour over the Nvidia affairs mirrors his conduct towards the war with Iran, Curlee argues, where he pressed ahead with military actions despite being forewarned of potential complications.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran contradicted advice that the country’s Islamic regime had the resilience to withstand attempts to topple it and was likely to retaliate by closing the strait of Hormuz – predictions that were subsequently borne out.

Trump’s dismissal of intelligence warnings in both cases recalls his comments at a 2018 summit with Vladimir Putin when he openly sided the Russian president over US intelligence agencies, who had assessed that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

His indifference to intelligence work and the professionals who perform it appears to surpass that of previous administrations, even those who were accused of deliberately politicizing the practice – an accusation leveled at George W Bush following the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

“There are other administrations that have ignored or or tried to politicize intelligence but I think the Trump administration stands alone in how little it seems to regard the intelligence analysis prepared to help the president make decisions,” said Curlee.

“The best example of this is the run-up to the war in Iran, where the administration just truly shut out the warnings which have been there and were provided for many years about what the Iranians would do in the case of a war.”

Trump’s administration has also fired agents for providing intelligence assessments at odds with the president’s own statements. Last year, Lt Gen Jeffrey Kruse, the head of the defense intelligence agency, was dismissed over a report that contradicted Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear sites had been “obliterated” by US strikes carried out in June 2025.

“What makes them really different from, say, the Bush administration, is that even that administration did not publicly fire officers when they didn’t provide information the president wanted to hear,” said Curlee, who also served on the White House national security council under Trump and Joe Biden.
“I feel pretty strongly that the fault of the Iran war lies at this refusal to listen to the intelligence community.”

Curlee said the Chinese acquisition of the Nvidia chips compared in strategic significance to the case of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, a US couple who were executed after being convicted of passing on atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the early years of the cold war. That made official indifference to the intelligence discovery all the more remarkable, she argued.

“This is a technology at the heart of the strategic competition with our primary competitor in the world, and at an industrial scale, they managed to divert chips from our leading hardware company,” she said.

“It’s a terrible thing that’s occurred and we can’t undo that. But uncovering it and stopping it was done at least over a year ago. If the policymaker then refuses to do their to do their job, there’s nothing the intelligence community can do about that.”
The administration’s stance has drawn further scrutiny by deciding not to provide a “defensive briefing” to Jensen Huang about the discovery.

“Before public accusations and scandals, it used to be accepted practice for someone to pull the American target aside for a man-to-man chat – to tell him to think with the head between his shoulders,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst specializing in Latin America who also has experience in Taiwan.

“The chat might even include discussion of feeding the foreigner some disinformation. It seems that four years of Trump first presidency, four years of do-nothingism with Biden, and now almost two years of Trump II have so deeply changed the intel community that practical solutions are no longer allowed.”
No explanation has been provided for the failure to warn Huang – thus allowing him to continue his relationship with Alice Huang. He was also allowed to maintain his already close access to Trump.

Curlee said it was a “policy decision [rather than] an intelligence decision.” She added “It is to me a very unusual suspect decision to let something like this go on for as long as it apparently did, without at minimum protecting this US citizen, who is the object of of a Chinese spy operation.”

Fevered speculation has swirled over whether Alice Huang may have been part of a “honey trap” operation set by China’s intelligence services to lure Jensen Huang into a close business relationship that would entice him into vast amounts of Nvidia’s coveted chips to a company which would them to pass them to China, subverting American law.

China’s sprawling Ministry of State Security [MSS] is believed to use the technique, which most western intelligence agencies publicly insist they do not use, on the grounds that is unethical and potentially counterproductive, because it often depends on blackmail.

But analysts doubt that it occurred in this instance. Alice Huang, they suggest, could have disclosed the relationship to Chinese agents after it began because she was legally obliged to do so under China’s catch-all intelligence law, which legally obliges the country’s citizens to “cooperate” with security services on matters defined as “national security”. That term has a much broader definition under China’s laws than in most western countries, and can cover commercial and economic development issues.
Frank Montoya, a retired Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent who specialized on China, said a straightforward “honey trap” was unlikely.

“I don’t think that it was it was mapped out specifically where the MSS officer said we’re going to find this person and we’re going to set her up for business and then target her against against the CEO of [Nvidia],” he said.

“There was a confluence of opportunities. She’s very ambitious, very smart and she has this idea, and doesn’t necessarily brings it to the MSS, but is talking to somebody else. She has connections in the party, and she’s talking to somebody else, and then somebody else talks to the MSS and says, ‘hey, let’s see if we can take advantage of that’.”

He added: “This was a multi-billion dollar purchase [of Nvidia chips]. There’s no way the MSS alone can fund that. They’re going to need somebody higher up [in the Chinese communist party] to not only approve that but to provide the money when the deal is made.”
The operation, Montoya said, bore the hallmarks of the Chinese espionage approach, which he described as “whole of government” and lacking the “clandestinity” of traditional spy craft.

Alice Huang would have drawn the attention of US intelligence agencies through Megaspeed’s mass purchase of Nvidia chips, and because it rented out services from its Singapore data centers to Chinese AI companies, Curlew argues.

The intimate nature of her relationship with Jensen Huang, and her links to Chinese intelligence is thought to have been discovered through surveillance of her phone, almost certainly carried out by the National Security Agency.

Trump has dismissed the case’s importance, saying he does not believe US national security was threatened and telling Fox News: “We spy on China. They spy on us.” He later told reporters that he raised the matter only briefly when he met China’s president, Xi Jinping, at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering Shenzhen.
It is an attitude Curlee lamented as disdainful of intelligence as a whole.

“We are spending tens of billions of dollars and people put their lives in jeopardy to collect information at great personal risk so that our leaders have decision-advantage, the ability to anticipate crises around the corner and can respond to foreign threats,” she said. “If the president can’t be bothered to listen to his intelligence community then what is what is the point of it all?”

articles.title: Germany's Wadephul 'shocked' by Trump's Nvidia intervention
articles.summary: The German foreign minister has criticized Donald Trump's interference in the chip-maker's economic activities. Jensen Huang was brought back after stepping down as Nvidia CEO amid multiple scandals.

image.caption: Wadephul was speaking at a conference in BerlinImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Tuesday expressed shock over US President Donald Trump's admission that he persuaded chip-producing giant Nvidia to reinstall ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia brought Huang back on Monday in a surprise decision, less than two weeks after the CEO stepped down amid a series of affairs.
What did Wadephul say about Trump's involvement in Nvidia?

"It shocked me, to be honest, because as far as I know, if I'm personally looking back, I have never seen or recognized such an intervention from the political side into a particular company," Wadephul told reporters at a foreign policy conference in Berlin.
"And I do have some doubts ⁠whether ​this is a very ​good model for the future," he added.
"But OK, that took place in the United States of America," the foreign minister said.
Wadephul went on to say there are enough reasons to defend the rules-based international order, and that includes political power not getting involved in the economic activities of companies.
Trump boasts about interference in Nvidia decision
Huang's shock reinstatement on Monday came on the back of a unanimous vote by Nvidia's board of directors.

The news was welcomed by Trump, who called it the "correct and proper decision" in a post on Truth Social. The president later said he had played a key role, having spoken "directly and indirectly" to the board of directors, urging them to reinstate the scandal-hit ex-CEO.
"I convinced them," Trump said. "I made the deal."

Huang came under massive fire after it was reported he had had an affair with the CEO of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. She was also accused of being a spy working on behalf of Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia's Cage for AI: can it prevent disaster?
Nvidia, Trump see stock surge after Huang's reinstallment

Nvidia's shares took a hit on Huang's stepping down, but rebounded by 30% on Monday after it was announced he was being reinstalled, adding over $900 billion (€820 billion) to the company's market value.
This share price surge also appears to have benefited Trump himself, with the Financial Times calculating that the president saw his Nvidia stock go up $15 million.

Huang's return has also brought some calm to the market that appeared to be teetering, with growing concerns about the viability of the AI sector, which now makes up a substantial part of the US stock market.
It also marks a turn around from the poor showing by Anthropic's IPO launch that saw its early gains quickly melt away amid fears that the AI sector has been overvalued.

articles.title: Land mine deaths reach five-year high, watchdog says
articles.summary: Myanmar reported the highest annual land mine casualty toll, followed by Syria and Afghanistan, ICBL report says. Since 1999, nearly 50 thousand people were killed by land mines.

image.caption: Land mines have been heavily used in Russia's war in UkraineImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa7picture alliance

blocks.text: Land mines killed or injured more people in 2025 than in any year since 2020, according to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines' (ICBL) annual report.

The report stated that the number of recorded deaths was at least 6,929, which is a 10% increase compared with last year. According to the campaign, four out of five victims were civilians, and half of those were minors.
Experts say the true figure is likely higher as not all land mine related death and injuries are recorded as such.
Myanmar reported the highest annual casualty toll for the third year in a row, with 1,891 victims, amid a "massive" new mine use.
In Syria, the number of casualties climbed by 50% to 1,602 in 2025, after the large-scale return of displaced people following the ousting of president Bashar Assad.
Myanmar and Syria were followed by Afghanistan with 497 casualties.
'The Ottawa Treaty faces its greatest test,' report warns
The ICBL criticized Ukraine, over its continued use of land mines. Ukraine, which is currently being invaded by Russia, is one of the 162 state parties to the Mine Ban Treaty.

The treaty, known as the Ottawa Treaty, prohibits the use, production, storage and transfer of anti-personnel mines. The treaty was ratified by 166 countries, but not by China, India, Russia, Israel, North Korea, or the US, along with nearly 30 others.
Land mines in Europe — the return of a banned weapon

Five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty last year: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland and Poland. Ukraine has also withdrawn, though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.
"The treaty’s norms face their greatest test since 1999," the report said, citing the withdrawals.
In 2025, Ukraine justified its move to withdraw from the treaty by citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines on Ukrainian territory.

The campaign said Ukraine was still "fully bound by the treaty" but had breached its ban on producing anti-personnel mines. It said the country had manufactured both 3D-printed mines and mines designed to be dropped by drones.
Report also noted that Russia has used antipersonnel land mines extensively in Ukraine since its full-scale invasion began in 2022.
Nearly 50 thousand people killed by land mines since 1999

Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Cambodia, Iraq, Morocco, North Korea, South Korea and Ukraine have "massive land mine contamination," meaning they have more than 100 square kilometers of land contaminated by land mines, the report assessed.

Since 1999, 49,859 people were killed and 118,525 injured by land mines, according to Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor, the research and monitoring arm of the ICBL, and the Cluster Munition Coalition NGOs.

articles.title: Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
articles.summary: A North Korean troop buildup Ukraine warned about months ago has yet to materialize, even as strategic cooperation goes on. Analysts say Pyongyang is balancing its ties with Moscow and Beijing.

image.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un commemorated troops killed in Ukraine earlier this yearImage: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.
However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.

Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.

He said a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy says North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.

However, Kovalenko added Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.
No need for North Korean reinforcements?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.
North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine
He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future plans.

Han said it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.

He told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he said, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.
North Korean weapons keep flowing
Ukrainian official Kovalenko said North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.
He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing new drones and missiles.
In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy said that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.

He warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs
Balancing Russia and China ties
Kovalenko said Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.
In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.

Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.
Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.

Ahn said that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing

Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.
By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.

Kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.

articles.title: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.summary: Andrei Chibis, head of Russia's northern Murmansk region, is the first governor to be detained for five years.

blocks.text: Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.
However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.
Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.
According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.
He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

articles.title: Leftwing coalition leader calls for rental revolution as Spain heads for snap election
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Ada Colau hopes public anger over housing will transfer into support for her Broad Front coalition in Sunday’s vote

The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called…

blocks.text: The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called for a drastic rethink of the country’s entire housing rental system, and described the eviction of an 87-year-old woman – the spark for nationwide protests that in turn triggered Sunday’s snap general election – as “the last straw” for desperate tenants.
“We’re not interested in small changes,” Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor, told the Guardian in an interview. “We want to reform the entire rental sector.”

Public outrage over the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid apartment in September prompted the government, led by Pedro Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE), to propose a series of changes to Spain’s housing laws. After the proposals were voted down by a combination of rightwing parties and Catalan nationalists, Sánchez called an election.

blocks.caption: Ada Colau said Broad Front support for a Socialist-led government would depend on it agreeing to expropriate properties owned by vulture funds. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters

blocks.text: “When Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who had paid rent all her life, was evicted out of pure greed, that lit the fuse,” said Colau, who stepped out of the political limelight three years ago after failing to win a third term as Barcelona mayor.

The Broad Front alliance was founded in February to unite parties to the left of the PSOE, and named Colau as its candidate for prime minister on 12 October. “When I saw how many people were taking to the streets that’s when I agreed to be a candidate,” she said. “I thought, if I can be useful now, I have to be involved 100%.”

Polls have indicated that the conservative People’s party (PP) will win the most seats in Sunday’s election, but will fall short of a parliamentary majority, meaning the far-right Vox party could become kingmakers. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would signal the return of the far right to government in Spain for the first time in the country’s post-dictatorship democratic history.

Colau’s alliance does not include the leftist group Podemos or the Catalan Republican Left (ERC) party. “I said to both Podemos and ERC we could change the front’s name, I offered to stand aside in favour of a consensus candidate, but the parties decided on a different strategy and I have to respect their decision,” Colau said.

Colau said she was sceptical of polls pointing to a PP-Vox majority. “I don’t think the majority of people want to go back to pre-democratic times,” she said. “People in the street don’t share this fatalism that the political right is going to win.

“People are very motivated, they’re very conscious that this isn’t an election like any other. This is the first time since the dictatorship that the far right might be in government and we might see the return of censorship, that we might see something like ICE in Spain, as well as attacks on groups such as the LGBT community and women.”

Polls suggest that a broad leftwing coalition encompassing the PSOE and all the smaller parties to the left of it won’t get enough votes to secure a parliamentary majority, but Colau is undeterred. She pointed out that at the general election in 2023 it was predicted that the right and far right would win, only for voters to return a progressive government, “admittedly with a very mixed and rather fragile parliamentary majority”.
She added: “At the moment we’re at about 8% and our goal is 10%. We believe people want to vote not just to keep out the far right, they want to vote for social progress.”
after newsletter promotion

Colau has been a housing activist for over 20 years, and says there is little to choose between the PP and PSOE on the issue, blaming both for the mortgage bubble that led to mass evictions after the 2008 financial crash and then allowing the current rental crisis to unfold.

“We’re not interested in small changes,” she said. “We want to reform the entire rental sector in line with something similar to Germany and, above all, get rid of the vulture funds that are destroying our neighbourhoods and driving us out of our cities. Vulture funds contribute nothing, everything they do is harmful.”

She said that 13 funds controlled about 100,000 properties, and that the Broad Front’s support for a Socialist-led government would depend on it agreeing to expropriate these properties “at a fair but not a market price”.

She said that when she was mayor she managed to increase the social housing stock by assuming control of more than 1,600 homes that were in the hands of big property owners. “If we could do that in Barcelona with fewer powers than the government, obviously it can be done at state level,” she said, adding that the constitution stated that housing was not only a right but that it must have a social function. “As for regulating rents, it isn’t such a radical proposal, it’s something that’s practised in various European countries.”

As mayor, Colau won international plaudits for her efforts to prioritise people over cars, but at home she was equally loved and loathed. During her time in office she came under constant attack from the pro-car lobby and faced over a dozen “lawfare” cases, all of which were rejected by the courts. Much of the hostility directed towards her was misogynist. “I’ve always said I’d only return to politics if I think I can be particularly useful, if not, I’ll do something else, because there are many ways to be political, not just in institutions,” she said. “If I can make a contribution now, I will do whatever I can to stop fascism returning to this country.”

articles.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.summary: Naeem Abu Nahel, who had only been in the position for two months, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's interior ministry says.

blocks.text: An Israeli air strike has killed the head of Hamas's internal security service in Gaza.

Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said Naeem Abu Nahel was targeted by an aircraft in western Gaza City. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel had been "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
Earlier, Palestinian first responders and health officials reported that six other people had been killed in two Israeli air strikes elsewhere in Gaza on Tuesday.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, they said. The other three, including two police officers, were killed in a separate strike on a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, condemned the second attack, saying it was "part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it had "struck terrorists in the area".
Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed by Israel and Hamas in October last year.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Pope Francis' diary reveals claims he saw the devil three times
articles.summary: Published extracts from the late pontiff's diary claim one of the visions happened "in the choir loft" during Mass.

blocks.text: Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.

In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.
"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.

In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.
Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign.
"Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry.
"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."
Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes.

"He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he said happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.
He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome.
"I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything," he wrote, adding that "the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters".

articles.title: Five women killed every hour by family members or partners — UN report
articles.summary: On average, 129 women or girls were killed every day in 2025 by someone in their close social circle, UN data showed.

image.caption: The UN report noted that women often face barriers to accessing the justice systemImage: Ihsaan Haffejee/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday.

This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report said ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.
The total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories. They translate to an average of 129 women and girls killed by their close social circle each day.
Africa recorded the highest number of femicides, at 22,100. Asia followed, with 15,100 victims, ahead of the Americas with 7,400, Europe with 2,100 and Oceania with 300.
Femicide is a hate crime broadly defined as "the intentional killing of women or girls because they are female."
Why so many women fear for their lives in South Africa
One in three women experienced physical or sexual violence
The report also found that although global homicide rates have declined, femicide rates have fallen at a slower pace, particularly in the Americas and Europe.
According to the UN, this shows the barriers women often face in accessing the justice system and that "these crimes are deeply rooted in social norms and gender stereotypes."
Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence, yet only 7% reported it to the police, a separate UN Women report found.

According to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, the number of women and girls killed by a family member or an intimate partner has wavered between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years.
Gang warfare in Ecuador fuels wave of femicides

"Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes 'tolerable,'" UNODC director Monica Juma said. "Changing this reality calls for sustained action across all levels of society."

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that the world needed to "act urgently to ensure no warning sign is ignored, no survivor is left without protection, and no perpetrator escapes accountability."

articles.title: Bombed factories, billion-dollar opportunity: Why German companies are staying in Ukraine
articles.summary: German companies remain committed to Ukraine despite million-dollar losses, an unreliable energy supply and a shortage of skilled workers. They are betting on new markets and long-term growth.

image.caption: Foreign companies operating in Ukraine see big opportunities, but also face substantial risksImage: Sergey Bobok/AFP

blocks.text: Power plants, train stations, shopping centers, warehouses and residential buildings: The massive Russian attacks on civilian targets across Ukraine continue unabated. Industrial facilities have also come under fire, affecting German companies.

"Over the past few months, goods and facilities worth several hundred million euros have gone up in smoke," reported Oliver Gierlichs, who heads Bayer's operations in Ukraine and serves as president of the German-Ukrainian Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK Ukraine). The damage is estimated at €500 million ($544 million).

At the 9th German-Ukrainian Business Forum, held in Berlin on November 20, Gierlichs described the situation on the ground. Together with two other German business associations, the AHK had invited around 500 participants from politics and industry, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.

According to the AHK, just over 2,000 German companies are active in Ukraine. German direct investment in the country totals around €1 billion ($1.1 billion). The situation remains critical due to the ongoing attacks, Gierlichs said. "We are preparing for a difficult winter."
Made in Germany — Rebuilding Ukraine
Ukrainian economy under pressure
After posting comparatively strong growth rates in recent years, Ukraine's economy has slowed sharply since the summer.

"The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and production capacity in recent months have significantly worsened the economic outlook," according to the latest analysis by the Kyiv School of Economics (KSE), which warns of "substantial risks."

Energy supplies are under strain, and electricity remains in short supply. Companies are also grappling with a worker shortage, as many people have been mobilized for military service or have fled abroad to escape the attacks. German business leaders also cite burdensome approval processes and unclear regulations in Ukraine.

"Not a single German company has left Ukraine since the start of this war," Merz emphasized at the business forum. He also pointed out that "in 2025, trade between Germany and Ukraine exceeded €12 billion, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year."
EU releases €3.2 billion from Ukraine recovery fund
Benefits extend beyond Ukraine

Military cooperation currently tops the agenda in German-Ukrainian relations. Germany continues to supply large quantities of defense equipment, but new capabilities are increasingly being developed through joint ventures. At the business forum, held at the House of German Business Associations in Berlin, the long-range combat drone "Anubis," produced by the German-Ukrainian joint venture Auterion Airlogix, was displayed in the foyer. The drone was developed in Ukraine and the software in Germany.

A total of 5,000 drones are to be produced near Munich. This marks the first time Germany has established industrial-scale production of heavy attack drones on its own soil. "Through this cooperation, Germany's technological capacity for innovation is expanding in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago," Merz said.

The chancellor is convinced that cooperation between the two countries will also benefit Germany's civilian industries. "What we invest in Ukraine today will be repaid many times over through stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and economic growth," he said.
Half a trillion dollars needed for reconstruction

For foreign companies operating in Ukraine, it is a continuous balancing act. On the one hand, substantial risks persist; on the other, Ukraine represents a land of opportunity, with a market size virtually unmatched anywhere else in Europe. In February 2025, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government estimated that Ukraine would need $524 billion in funding for reconstruction and recovery over the following 10 years. This figure has likely grown even larger since then.

In this context, Ukraine is increasingly seen not merely as a recipient of aid but also as a potential future business destination. The country aims to modernize its economy, bring it into alignment with EU standards, and achieve deeper integration into the European single market over the long term.
Can Ukraine still count on Germany?
Mechanical engineering, energy and infrastructure opportunities
"We see significant opportunities in the defense industry, the energy sector, infrastructure, information technology and many other industries," Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi said in Berlin.

"German expertise and Ukrainian drive, combined with unity and determination, make for a powerful partnership," Oliver Gierlichs noted. However, achieving this will require greater support, the AHK president emphasized. "Companies need reliable financing and investment guarantees, as well as effective instruments to protect themselves against war-related risks."
Reliable logistics, predictable business conditions, and faster administrative procedures will also be essential, he added.
Investment guarantees and reforms as prerequisites for new projects

At the business forum, Chancellor Merz pledged support in these areas while also calling on Ukraine to pursue further reforms, particularly to strengthen the rule of law and combat corruption. "These reforms are a prerequisite for additional financial assistance and investment."

Another challenge stems from the differing interests of the partners. German companies are seeking to expand into new markets, while their Ukrainian counterparts seek technology transfers and local production to keep as much value creation as possible in the country. "Export fees or legal restrictions on the transfer of intellectual property rights stand in the way of joint innovation efforts," the chancellor cautioned.
High-tech revolution in defense
Who is financing Ukraine's reconstruction?

Representatives of Ukrainian business associations estimate that the private sector could cover up to 40% of Ukraine's reconstruction costs in the long term. For now, however, many projects rely on support from international development banks, government guarantees, or public funding programs. Without such support, many investments would be difficult to undertake.

In principle, business investment follows a straightforward model: Companies commit their own capital and bear the losses if a venture fails commercially. When bank loans are involved, the risk is initially shared by the company and the lending institution. Government-backed projects are different. When investment guarantees are in place, companies are compensated for any losses incurred.

This does not apply when companies incur losses as a result of their own business decisions. Compensation may, however, be available in cases involving political actions, such as expropriation, or when war destroys assets and disrupts operations. Under a government guarantee, the taxpayer ultimately bears the risk in such circumstances. By the end of 2025, the German government had provided investment guarantees covering a total investment volume of €558 million ($611 million) in Ukraine.

German companies hoping to benefit from Ukraine's reconstruction need to establish partnerships and build a long-term presence in the country now. After all, the competition is already heating up. At the German-Ukrainian Business Forum, participants noted that German business leaders have often been more risk-averse than their counterparts from Turkey, India and China. International interest in Ukraine's reconstruction is considerable, and German companies are far from the only ones vying for contracts.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
articles.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than…

image.caption: One day green, the next day red — global stock markets have swung wildly in recent monthsImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.
Will Anthropic put profits over security?
How passive investing is fueling the AI trade
The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.
These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

blocks.caption: The rise of neo-stock brokers, like Trade Republic in Europe, has spurred public interest in investingImage: Claudia Nass/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: Riding the winners works — until it doesn't
Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.
The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.
The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.
Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.
Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.
Don't put all your chips in AI stocks
"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.
"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."
Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.
Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

blocks.caption: President Donald Trump has pressured TSMC to move some chip production from Taiwan to the USImage: Cheng-Chia Huang/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: How funds fuel investor hubris
That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.
"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.
When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.
"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."
Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia
To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.
In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.
EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.
Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments?
AI crash will have ripple effects

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.
Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."
LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

articles.title: German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award
articles.summary: Two German film students confronted the American who won festival prizes with their animated movie. "The Talented Mr. F," their documentary on their fight against plagiarism, is now in the spotlight.

image.caption: The movie 'Butty' was suddenly called 'T-130'Image: MDR/Neue Flimmer GmbH

blocks.text: It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.
Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

When the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale quickly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.
How could that have happened?

US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.
A story turned into a documentary, 'The Talented Mr. F'

Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

blocks.caption: Moritz (l) and Julius on a research trip to New York  Image: MDR/Benedikt Hugendubel

blocks.text: "We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it."
The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.
"We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person."
Fascination instead of anger

While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.

The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

blocks.caption: Julius and Moritz gather information about Samuel FelintonImage: MDR/Benedikt Hugendubel

blocks.text: The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.
Sue or stay creative?
Later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.
"The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts."

"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story."

blocks.caption: Samuel Felinton says he doesn't want to be 'forgotten'Image: MDR/Neue Flimmer GmbH

blocks.text: And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.
They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge."

The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.
Award-winning works
Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

For the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.
And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

blocks.caption: The team celebrating their International Emmy Award for the documentaryImage: Anne Pollmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Don't be afraid to show yourselves'
Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.
Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.
The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.
They have a clear message for young creatives.

"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors."
What started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.
This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

articles.title: Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord
articles.summary: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops detained 'El Chapo Isidro', who had managed to evade capture for years.

blocks.text: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.
The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.
Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
The arrest of Meza Flores in the northern Sinaloa state sparked a wave of unrest, which led to eight alleged drug cartel members being detained for their involvement in the retaliatory violence.

articles.title: Russian drone violates Polish airspace days after cruise missiles fell on country – Europe live
articles.summary:
Authorities investigating ‘intentional activity’ amid growing tensions between Moscow and countries on Nato’s eastern flank

Meanwhile, the Financial Times is reporting this morning…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 17m agoUS delaying delivery of much-needed Patriot air defence missiles - media report
27m agoMorning opening: Poland investigating (another) brief airspace violation by Russian drone

blocks.text: US delaying delivery of much-needed Patriot air defence missiles - media report
Meanwhile, the Financial Times is reporting this morning that the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of about 60 much-needed Patriot air defence interceptors to Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian service members walk next to a launcher of a Patriot air defence system, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in an undisclosed location, Ukraine. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: The interceptors, paid for by Ukraine’s western allies, are reportedly being held up by the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, who needs to sign off on their re-export, three people told the newspaper.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has repeatedly warned of the urgent need for more air defence missiles to protect the skies above Ukraine as the country braces for a difficult winter, with Russia continuing its strikes on critical civilian infrastructure.
Morning opening: Poland investigating (another) brief airspace violation by Russian drone

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

A suspected Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace during strikes on western Ukraine on Monday night in what authorities have described as “intentional activity” by Moscow – just days after three cruise missiles fell in Poland during a major attack on Ukraine.
The drone, believed to be carrying surveillance equipment, remained in Polish airspace for eight minutes before flying back to Ukraine.
Poland’s deputy defence minister, Paweł Zalewski, told RMF24 that the military decided against shooting it down because of risks to civilian properties in the area.

The incident took place just hours after Nato held emergency talks over last week’s airspace breach, authorising the deployment of a Nato Airborne Warning and Control System, AWACS, aircraft to Poland.

It also comes amid growing tensions between Russia and countries on the eastern flank of Nato, with Moscow making unsubstantiated accusations against Estonia warning that it’s acting ‘on verge of unleashing open war,” and a growing diplomatic spat with Finland.
Overnight, at least two people were killed and 40 injured in Russian attacks on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia ⁠overnight, with further attacks reported in the Sumy region.
I will keep an eye on this for you.
It’s Tuesday, 24 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: DR Congo says aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
articles.summary: A South African fighter pilot and a Ugandan officer are reportedly among those aboard the downed plane.

blocks.text: The Democratic Republic of Congo says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebels' claim.
It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.
Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.
A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".
Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".
"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.
The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.
Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.
Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.
The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

articles.title: What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
articles.summary: Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is…

image.caption: The US detonated the weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above Earth, creating an artificial aurora visible from HawaiiImage: U.S. Air Force 1352nd Photographic Group, Lookout Mountain Station/US Govt. Defense Threat Reduction Agency

blocks.text: A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.
We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.
What does history teach us?

On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.
An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.
How does the physics change in space?

The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

blocks.caption: The glow over Honolulu lasted about seven minutes, but radiation from the blast damaged satellites months laterImage: US Federal Government/Public Domain

blocks.text: Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.
Which systems would be exposed?

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.
Is it legal, and could it be detected?
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.
The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.
Can the US protect itself?

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.
AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs?

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.
Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.
Could radioactive fallout reach the ground?

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.
As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

articles.title: Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK
articles.summary:
Saurav Das was due to give talks at UK universities on protest movement but says ‘coward government’ prevented him flying

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was…

blocks.text: A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was prevented from leaving Delhi to fly to the UK to give talks on the viral group’s protests.

Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers since its launch in May. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.
The incident comes a month after he was detained for defying a security crackdown in Delhi during protests demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.

“This coward government did not allow me to board my flight to London where I was invited by prestigious universities like Oxford, Cambridge, LSE (London School of Economics), Edinburgh to deliver talks on the Cockroach movement,” Das said in a social media post late on Monday. “Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual government was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions.”
Das was due to speak at the Oxford Union society on 1 December.
CJP-organised protests in July over alleged examination irregularities forced the education minister to resign, marking a rare climbdown by the government of Narendra Modi.

Critics say human rights and press freedoms have declined since Modi came to power in 2014. Earlier this month, India barred more than 100 foreign speakers from attending a democracy summit organised by the opposition Congress party. Those denied visas included a Norwegian journalist who had previously questioned Modi about press freedom.
