In 2022, authorities prevented Sanna Irshad Mattoo, an award-winning photographer from India-administered Kashmir, from flying to the US to collect her Pulitzer prize.

articles.title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
articles.summary:
A campaign securing the landmark return to India of ancestral remains taken during British colonial rule has opened a wider conversation about restitution

The lacerating legacy of…

blocks.text: The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects.
For almost 80 years, human remains were displayed on crowded glass shelves at Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University, one of the world’s most celebrated institutions.

Many of them were, in fact, skeletal remains taken from Nagaland brought to the museum by two British colonial administrators, John Henry Hutton and James Philip Mills between 1910 and 1940. Now, after six years of consultations, negotiations and a concerted effort to build consensus across Naga communities, 39 skeletal remains are finally coming home. In early November, the museum handed custodianship to a Naga delegation of leaders and scholars. The repatriated remains include those of two children, a woman and a village chief.

“This is the first such repatriation of human remains to India,” Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist and professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told me. She had contacted the Pitt Rivers Museum in 2020 after reading in the Guardian that the museum was removing human remains from public display following an ethical review, setting the repatriation process in motion. In a statement, the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven, acknowledged that it has been a “long journey”, adding that “hope is possible as we work towards reconciliation and healing”.

blocks.caption: Members of the Naga delegation in Oxford, where the university transferred custodianship. Photograph: FNR RRaD Pictures

blocks.text: The review was part of a broader reassessment of the museum’s display practices and how it presented human remains from communities across the world. Among its most contentious displays were the shrunken heads known as tsantsa, from the Shuar people in South America. Pitt Rivers – one of the world’s leading anthropology and ethnography museums – has acknowledged that its display reinforced racist stereotypes about the culture. The Naga remains were displayed alongside artefacts and human remains from a number of communities, including from Nigeria and Papua New Guinea.

Naga academics have challenged the perception that the remains were exclusively associated with the practice of headhunting. While Naga warriors traditionally collected the heads of enemies killed in raids, the anthropologists say that British collectors acquired Naga human remains under duress during colonial expeditions.

For the Naga community, that was just the beginning of a long journey. India, unlike countries such as Australia, Canada and the US, has no national laws for the repatriation of Indigenous ancestral remains, says Kikon. “We had to ensure the process was community-led, in the absence of a policy and make sure the focus remained on healing and reconciliation. It was all unprecedented.”

The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a collective working toward peace and reconciliation among Naga Indigenous communities, facilitated the repatriation, and a voluntary research group, Recover, Restore and Decolonise (RRaD), was formed to build wider community awareness. Its volunteers travelled to urban centres and villages, talking with students, elders and intergenerational audiences about the human remains kept at the museum and what the community wanted to do with them.

The museum still has around 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. It also has 6,500 Naga objects, including clothing items, weapons, vessels and musical instruments, many from Mills and Hutton, while some items, like weapons, were bought from auction houses. “The Pitt Rivers Museum has one of the largest collections of Naga objects, artefacts and human remains in the world. What we have focused on for now is the skeletal remains, but this is only a first step in thinking more broadly about these collections,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at Edinburgh University.

The question of restitution of Indian artefacts and cultural heritage items has long occupied a prominent place in public discourse. At its heart is the Koh-i-noor diamond, which passed through Mughal, Persian and Afghan hands before Britain wrested it from the 10-year-old king, Maharaja Duleep Singh. Today, it is part of the British crown jewels, a symbol of the plunder of the empire and, for many in India, a theft that continues to rankle. Last year, an Indian parliamentary committee recommended establishing a dedicated heritage recovery taskforce to pursue the return of cultural objects held abroad, particularly those taken during the colonial period.

In the case of the human remains, the question is about the right to honour the ancestors and give them a dignified resting place. “How we imagine a shared future depends on how we understand our history. We have to look back and make sense of the past in order to think about the kind of future we want to create,” Longkumer told me.
“The Naga repatriation addresses a very deep colonial violence,” Kikon says. “It is about the dehumanisation where the remains of human beings were stored in museums and exhibited as exotic objects.”

The return prompted Kikon to reflect on the contradiction between the longstanding reverence for Oxford University by Indians, many of whom have aspired to study there, and the institution’s history of exhibiting the remains of their ancestors. “Repatriation is not just about bringing back bones. It was about starting a process of deep introspection,” she says. “Ultimately, it leaves us with a greater responsibility to reflect on how we live our lives.”
The remains will be buried at Naga Solidarity Park in Kohima, the capital of Nagaland.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A courtroom sketch of Nikhil Gupta in New York in 2024. Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/Reuters

blocks.text: Crime | A federal judge in New York sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to almost 20 years in prison for an assassination plot against the Khalistan separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, an American citizen. The prosecutors argued that Gupta had been directed by an Indian government employee, a charge that India denies.

Politics | In a new report, Human Rights Watch argued that India’s democratic institutions have been systematically hollowed out under the Modi government, which has used state agencies to target critics, undermined parliamentary oversight and promoted Hindu majoritarianism. Based on dozens of interviews, and drawing from news reports, HRW describes these actions as part of a broader authoritarian move to concentrate executive power.

Arts | The second edition of the India Biennale, organised by the Ministry of Culture, begins in Delhi on 4 December. Highlights include photographer Dayanita Singh’s work on show at Humayun’s Tomb and artist Paresh Maity and fashion designer Ritu Beri’s installation at Qutub Minar.
after newsletter promotion
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Barefoot College brings solar-powered lighting to rural areas. Photograph: Rebecca Conway/Getty Images

blocks.text: Writer Gayatri Rangachari Shah, a founding member of the Women Leadership Circle, recommends an inspiring model of rural development. “If there is an institution that captures an alternative vision of India, it’s the Barefoot College in Rajasthan. Set up by Sanjit ‘Bunker’ Roy in 1972, it has spent more than five decades putting rural communities at the centre of their own development. Its Solar Mamas programme has enabled women of all ages who had never been to school to learn to make and install solar lights. Its other initiatives include digital learning centres for young women, night schools for those working during the day, menstrual-friendly toilets in government schools, rainwater harvesting, waste management and recycling.
Roy died on 10 November but he passed on his work to a younger team.”
Count it

blocks.caption: The National Chambal Sanctuary is one of the areas where wildlife clearances were granted. Photograph: Hira Punjabi/Alamy

blocks.text: India’s top wildlife body approved the clearance of ecologically sensitive land and wildlife corridors covering an area of at least 99,000 hectares (244,530 acres) – an area about a third larger than Singapore – between 2014 and 2026, an analysis by Article 14 concluded. Defence projects, mining and irrigation were the top sectors for which the board granted clearances at the expense of forests and wildlife habitats, according to the investigation by Prakriti Srivastava and Prerna Singh Bindra.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: GTA VI has brought Disco Jazz to new audiences. Photograph: YouTube

blocks.text: Grand Theft Auto VI, billed as the biggest cultural event of the year, has smashed sales records. It has also helped propel a little-known 1982 Indian disco track to global fandom. Aaj Shanibar by the Bengali singer Rupa Biswas features on Worldwide FM, one of the radio stations in the game.

The song was part of an album called Disco Jazz that Biswas recorded during a visit to her brother in Canada. The album never made a splash and faded into obscurity, but years later her son discovered the track had found a following in DJ sets and was reissued by the US label Numero Group. Now, with GTA VI, the song has reached a generation who were not even born when the original was released 44 years ago.

articles.title: What China's Xi could take away from Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
articles.summary: Huang being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.

Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.

Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.

For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.

The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.

Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.

The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.

The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.

He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.

If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

articles.title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
articles.summary: Hasina has spoken several times of her desire to return, but this is the first time she has set a date.

blocks.text: Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.

The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

articles.title: Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy
articles.summary: According to a study by the Körber Foundation, a growing number of Germans now oppose providing military aid to Ukraine. The majority also believes that Germany should take a neutral position between…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has insisted on German support for Ukraine's war effort against RussiaImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.
Growing numbers of Germans oppose international engagement

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."
Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.
No longer a majority in favor of military aid to Ukraine

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.
As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."
The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).
Overwhelming majority wants Germany to remain neutral between the US and China

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.
"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.
If Europe wants independence, why does it keep turning to the US?
Should Germany always stand by Israel? Now only a third agree

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Malaysia to send thousands of migrants back to Myanmar as PM acknowledges junta’s ‘atrocities’
articles.summary:
Prime minister Anwar Ibrahim’s announcement comes days after the ICJ found Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya minority

Malaysia says it will send thousands of migrants and…

blocks.text: Malaysia says it will send thousands of migrants and refugees back to Myanmar, despite acknowledging that many asylum seekers in the country had been victims of “atrocities” carried ​out by the junta in Naypyidaw.
The announcement comes just days after the UN’s highest court ruled Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

Malaysia’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, said on Tuesday that the deportations were in line with advice from the international court of justice (ICJ), which was “to guarantee a safe and dignified return” for those fleeing persecution, and his country had not abandoned its principles of upholding the rights of the people of Myanmar.
The UN has previously warned that migrants sent back to Myanmar could face a dangerous homecoming.

It is unclear how many Rohingya, a Muslim minority group, are among those facing deportation. However, the Rohingya make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the UN. Many of the Rohingya escaped to Malaysia during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.

Anwar acknowledged that many asylum seekers in Malaysia were “victims of atrocities carried ​out by the Myanmar regime”, but said Malaysia could ‌no longer afford to host refugees. Hoping for them to be resettled in third countries had not worked, he said.

Many in Malaysia have grown increasingly frustrated by ‌the presence of refugees in the country, saying that hosting them has become a financial burden and a security risk, with a rise in anti-migrant sentiment in the country.

On Tuesday Anwar told Malaysia’s parliament that three naval ships would return 1,500 people in December, with an additional 5,303 people flown back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government.
Tuesday’s announcement follows last week’s ICJ ruling in The Hague that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ had never previously found a state responsible for genocide, and the judgment ended a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang rapes and burnt-down villages.
In its judgment, the ICJ said Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.
In September, Malaysia began sending back a group of about 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched its contested repatriation plan.
Malaysia’s government said in a statement at the time that the repatriation was necessary to resolve the “legacy issue” of foreign asylum seekers in Malaysia – of which it said 95% were from Myanmar.

“This long-standing issue has imposed a significant financial burden on the nation, triggered serious social crises, and created tangible security threats for the Malaysian people,” the statement said.
The UN had urged Malaysia to stop that repatriation, saying nobody should be deported to Myanmar, given the severity of the situation on the ground.
In late October, the Malaysian government said it would seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned were being held in military detention.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: India's 'cockroach' party leader says he was stopped from flying to UK
articles.summary: Saurav Das said that immigration authorities at Delhi airport told him that his passport had been "flagged".

blocks.text: A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.

"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

articles.title: South Korea tells island residents to take shelter after Russian military aircraft approach
articles.summary:
The order was issued after aircraft entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the island of Ulleungdo

Residents of a remote South Korean island were ordered to take shelter…

blocks.text: Residents of a remote South Korean island were ordered to take shelter on Tuesday morning after several Russian military aircraft came close to entering its airspace, prompting a pre-emptive alert from the military that anticipated a violation.
The defence ministry said it would summon the Russian defence attaché on Tuesday afternoon to lodge a strong protest.

The joint chiefs of staff (JCS) said the aircraft had entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan – known in South Korea as the East Sea – and approached the island of Ulleungdo. It did not specify how many Russian aircraft were involved, but South Korean air force jets were scrambled before the aircraft left.

A JCS spokesperson, Jang Do-young, said the aircraft had approached “to the point just before violating Ulleungdo’s airspace” and that, because military aircraft move very fast, a violation was anticipated.
The alert was issued pre-emptively to protect residents, he said.

The interior ministry issued the emergency alert at 7.52am to residents of Ulleungdo, a volcanic island of about 8,700 people 120km off the east coast, telling them to take shelter. The English portion of the message read: “EVACUATION, AIR RAID”.

Television broadcasts were interrupted by on-screen warnings telling residents to “prepare to evacuate to a nearby underground shelter facility and listen to broadcasting”. The alert was lifted at 7.55am.

On the island, sirens sounded and residents reportedly heard the noise of fighter jets. Jeong Hae-seung, 41, who was working on a building site, told the Hankyoreh newspaper he ran out of his workplace the moment the text arrived.

blocks.caption: A man jogs past a lighthouse at Jeodong port on the island of Ulleungdo. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I went outside wondering what on earth was going on, and the civil defence broadcast was playing, but I couldn’t make out what it was saying,” he said.
Baek Un-bae, who lives on the island, told broadcaster YTN that an elderly resident had telephoned him asking whether war had broken out.
“Older people have no access to the media, so all they hear is the warning broadcast and they are too alarmed to know what to do,” he said.
Others said they did not hear the sirens at all, with windows shut against the cold and strong winds blowing.
A second message, sent by North Gyeongsang province, which administers Ulleungdo, said a flying object “presumed to be a North Korean aircraft” had left the danger zone.
The province said it had mistakenly taken the wording from its routine drill messages, changed only the time and sent it in error.
Jang described the alert as unusual but said he could not confirm whether it was the first of its kind.
Tuesday’s incident was the fourth known entry by Russian military aircraft into the zone this year and the second in a week.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace, but countries establish such zones beyond their own airspace to identify incoming military flights early. While submitting a flight plan in advance is international practice, entering an identification zone without prior notification does not in itself violate international law.
Russia argues that the Korean zone has no basis in international law and does not recognise Seoul’s authority over it, and has repeatedly flown into it without notice.
According to data submitted to parliament, about 60 Russian entries without prior notification were recorded in the five years to 2024, compared with about 430 by Chinese aircraft.

Seoul previously summoned Russia’s defence attaché in March 2025 after eight entries in 10 days. At the time, it was the first such summons since a Russian aircraft violated South Korean airspace in 2019 and South Korean jets fired warning shots.

articles.title: Myanmar has been found guilty of genocide. Should Israel be worried? – podcast
articles.summary: The international court of justice has for the first time ruled that a state has committed genocide. Yasmin Ullah explains what it means for the Rohingya people, while…
articles.byline: Presented by Annie Kelly with Kaamil Ahmed, produced by George McDonagh, Harriet Mogie and Rudi Zygadlo

blocks.text: For seven years, Yasmin Ullah had been part of the delegation arguing that Myanmar had committed genocide – one of the gravest human rights crimes – against Rohingya Muslims.

The genocide has directly affected Yasmin and her family. Last week she was in court to hear the international court of justice’s landmark verdict against Myanmar. “I was really kind of pinching myself. It felt like we were all able to breathe again,” she tells Annie Kelly.

The verdict could have far-reaching consequences – especially for Israel, which is also facing a genocide case at the ICJ. The Guardian journalist Kaamil Ahmed explains how the case unfolded and what could happen next.

articles.title: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.summary:
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says

A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying…

blocks.text: A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.
The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.
The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.
The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.summary: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.

blocks.text: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

articles.title: How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
articles.summary: BBC's Lily Jamali reports from Nvidia's headquarters, where she gauges the reaction to Huang's return after Trump says he brokered a deal.

blocks.text: Nvidia's board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and president on Monday. President Trump has claimed credit for brokering the deal. What is the mood at Nvidia following the announcement? BBC's Lily Jamali reports from Nvidia's headquarters, where she gauges the reaction to Huang's return.
Video edited by Mabel Pickering

articles.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
articles.summary: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
articles.byline: Nomsa Maseko, Thuthuka Zondi, Eleanor Smallwood

blocks.text: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student
ByNomsa MasekoThuthuka Zondi and Eleanor Smallwood BBC World ServiceReporting fromEkurhuleni
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

blocks.text: Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

blocks.text: Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

blocks.text: Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.
She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.
When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.
"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.
She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.
Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.
In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.
She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.
Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

blocks.text: Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles
In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.
She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.
Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.
"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

blocks.text: Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed
Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.
Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.
Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.
Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

articles.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
articles.summary:
Carney watches on as comedian lampoons US leader and his interest in men’s backsides at correspondents’ event Ottawa

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a…

blocks.text: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.

With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.

He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”

He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.

The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

articles.title: 11-year-old Carly Rae Jepsen song surges up the charts thanks to GTA VI needle drop
articles.summary: Justin Bieber, Tate McRae, April Wine and other acts are also featured in the game.

image.caption: Carly Rae Jepsen's track Run Away With Me is getting a streaming bump 11 years after its release. (Vanessa Heins)

blocks.text: Music
Justin Bieber, Tate McRae, April Wine and other acts are also featured in the game.
Justin Bieber, Tate McRae, April Wine and other acts are also featured in the game
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 23, 2026 5:17 PM EST | Last Updated: 3 hours ago
Carly Rae Jepsen's saxophone-backed track Run Away With Me is getting a boost more than a decade after its release, thanks to its inclusion in the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

The song, originally released in 2015, is taking on a new life with a surprise remix in the game: between Nov. 16-22, there was a week over week increase of 157 per cent for listens to Run Away With Me on Spotify.
"Secret's finally out! GTA 6 let's run away together," Jepsen wrote on Instagram.
In a special mission sequence in the game, the song plays while the characters Jason and Lucia ride Sea-Doos.

Jepsen's fans have reacted across social media, with several commenting on YouTube under the music video for the song. "This scene in that mission had me floating bro," wrote @VincentNNS, while @voxious07 wrote, "I love how everyone felt the same feeling at that mission, it was surreal. What a game. What a song. What an experience."
The Weeknd's music also appeared in Vice City, courtesy of French electronic duo Justice.
The Toronto superstar is credited on My Only Vice, an unreleased track featured in the score for the long-awaited video game.

The song is among several original compositions credited to Justice, who created the game's main score. Rockstar Games lists the Weeknd, born Abel Tesfaye, as a co-writer alongside Justice members Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay.
The collaboration follows their work together on Wake Me Up, a track from the Weeknd’s 2025 album Hurry Up Tomorrow.

The Weeknd’s 2013 track Wanderlust is also featured on Flash FM, one of the game's fictional radio stations, alongside fellow Canadian Tate McRae's Sports car and Justin Bieber's 2017 collaboration with BloodPop, Friends.
Toronto rap star Drake also has several tracks in the game, including Nonstop, Nokia and Love Me, his collaboration with Lil Wayne and Future.
His 2013 hit Hold On, We're Going Home, featuring Toronto R&B duo Majid Jordan, is also included.
The official score for GTA VI is set to be released Dec. 11.
Toronto instrumental jazz group BadBadNotGood is featured on Leonida Jazz Radio with Blowin’ Smoke, an apparently unreleased collaboration with American trumpeter Randy Brecker.
Electronic artists also received a boost

Over on Stockyard FM, Vancouver-bred electronic duo Bob Moses appear with their Elderbrook collaboration Inner Light, which gained renewed attention after being featured in a GTA VI trailer earlier this year.
The Grammy-nominated pair, Tom Howie and Jimmy Vallance, told the Canadian Press that the song had racked up more than 50 million new streams since the trailer's release in August.
The duo’s track Nothing But You, remixed by DJ Tennis, is also included in the game, along with Never Come Back by Dundas, Ont.-born electronic artist Caribou.
Montreal metal vets Voivod also get some shine in the game, with their track Panorama featuring on The Chamber 106.6, a heavy music station.
Flip the dial to V-Rock, and you’ll hear Roller by Halifax rock greats April Wine, as well as Loverboy’s ubiquitous ’80s anthem Working for the Weekend.
Montreal-based producer Martyn Bootyspoon is among the musicians credited with contributing to the game's supplemental score.

Music has long been integral to the GTA experience, with the franchise’s fictional radio stations exposing generations of players to an eclectic mix of sounds as they cruise city streets and flee the cops.
Bob Moses said they were paid a relatively modest licensing fee, but the payoff was in the exposure to their music.
“I forget how much money it was, but it’s not enough to remember,” said Howie.
“The opportunity is definitely in the potential for the reach, not in the paycheque.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alex Nino Gheciu is a reporter with The Canadian Press.
With files from CBC Music

articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
articles.summary: The publisher of an essay on coercive control apologises for "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

blocks.text: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.
French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.
In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.
"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.
Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.
French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.
Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".
Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.
Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.
Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.
If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Iranian singer and four others receive lashes after performance without hijab
articles.summary:
Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law

An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each…

blocks.text: An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for “offending public decency by producing and ⁠publishing obscene and ⁠immoral ​content online”, an Iranian news website said on Monday.
Parastoo Ahmadi and the four ⁠others were also handed two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and travel, the Emtedad website ⁠quoted lawyer Mostafa Nili as saying.

The case followed the ​release of a ‌video on YouTube ‌in December 2024 showing Ahmadi performing without the mandatory hijab alongside ‌male musicians in Qom, south of the capital Tehran, Norway-based human rights group Hengaw said.

Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law. Iran rejects accusations over ‌its human rights record, saying western countries should focus on their own human rights ​problems.

Rules requiring women to wear the hijab were a flashpoint during protests in 2022 after the ⁠death in custody of Kurdish Iranian woman Mahsa Amini, ​who was ​arrested for allegedly violating ​the dress code.
The rules have increasingly been ​flouted on ‌the streets of Tehran ​and ​beyond, and enforcement of the rules has also become more selective.

articles.title: Israel seeks to jail Palestinian student activist without trial after dorm arrest
articles.summary:
Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations

Israeli professors, students and rights activists are…

blocks.text: Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.
Police took Tounsi, 26, a criminology and sociology student from East Jerusalem who is active in Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, from his dorm room on 8 November.
When he appeared by video link at a court hearing on 19 November he had visible bruises on his face, did not have the glasses he needs to see properly, and his hair and beard had been shaved.

Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, in the patrol car and at the police station, Israeli media reported. Interrogators questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.
Both groups called for his immediate release and warned against using security agencies to silence political activity and critical speech.

“[This] could happen to any student and any one of us, especially in a month when the government is persecuting Arab citizens, from [journalist] Abed Abu Shehadeh to the leaders of Arab political parties,” Standing Together said in a statement, calling on the university to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process.

Ir Amim described Tounsi as thoughtful, gentle and a valued partner “in movements bringing Palestinians and Israelis together”, in a statement that also warned of “serious concerns for his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process”.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators call for the release of Mahdi Tounsi outside the Jerusalem district court. Photograph: Jess Flom/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: After losing the election, Netanyahu and his allies weaponised false accusations of mass fraud – Israel’s election commission validated the results – in an attempt to hold on to power by delegitimising the votes of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The prime minister has also been accused of politicising security institutions in his campaign against Palestinian-led parties, and fostering a rise in racist rhetoric.

When police powers to hold Tounsi under the original arrest warrant expired last week, they submitted an order to hold him without trial in administrative detention, signed by the defence minister, Israel Katz.

The administrative detention law allows Israel to hold individuals for up to six months without charging them or allowing them to see evidence against them, although it has to be presented in a closed court.
Because the Shin Bet security force did not send a representative to the hearing on Tounsi’s detention last week, it was postponed until Tuesday.

Ahead of the court hearing, Jewish and Palestinian students demonstrated at universities across the country, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, with signs including “Free Mahdi” and “Kidnapping Palestinians will not silence justice”.
The university authorities did not inform his family, and his detention only came to light after concerned friends reported him missing.

Hebrew University said in a statement that it was notified about the arrest shortly before police seized Tounsi, that no university representatives were present when he was detained and police afterwards said the arrest took place “without unusual incidents”.
It did not directly address the allegations of police violence, his visible bruising, the shaving of his head and beard, removal of his glasses or the shifting legal framework.

“The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings,” the statement said.
“We are concerned for his wellbeing,” the statement added, saying the university hoped “that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process”.
Israeli police did not respond to requests for comment about Tounsi’s detention.

Tounsi is a resident of East Jerusalem, not a Palestinian citizen of Israel. Palestinians holding that status can move freely inside Israel and Jerusalem but are stateless and can not vote in Israeli national elections.
